## pvConvertIntoMolecule

Turns a point set (polydata, unstructured grid or another vtkPointSet) into a molecule (vtkMolecule): every point becomes an atom at the same position, its element read from a one-component point array of atomic numbers, and the other point arrays become atom data. ## pvConvertSelection

Converts a selection (a vtkSelection on the Input port, e.g. from pvIDSelectionSource or pvLocationSelectionSource) into another content type, evaluated against the dataset on DataInput: for example cell indices become the global IDs, or the values of a named array, at those cells. The output is again a vtkSelection with no geometry; feed it to pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. vtkConvertSelection can produce INDICES, GLOBALIDs, PEDIGREEIDS or VALUES from another type; FRUSTUM, LOCATIONS and THRESHOLDS are only accepted when the input selection already has that type.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView 5.13.3 initializes OutputType to LOCATIONS, which cannot be produced from any other selection type; always set OutputType, usually to INDICES, GLOBALIDs or VALUES.
- VALUES output needs at least one name in ArrayNames and THRESHOLDS exactly one; otherwise the native filter reports an error.
- GLOBALIDs and PEDIGREEIDS output read the designated global-ID or pedigree-ID array of the DataInput dataset; datasets without one cannot be converted.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvCriticalTime

Scans every time step of a temporal input and records, for each point or cell, the first time value at which the selected array meets a threshold criterion (above, below or between thresholds; comparisons include the threshold values). The result is a static (non-temporal) dataset with one array named <array>_critical_time; other point and cell arrays are dropped, and entries whose criterion is never met are NaN. Use it for arrival or exceedance maps, e.g. when temperature first exceeds a limit. The mesh must keep the same points and cells over time.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The filter executes the whole upstream pipeline for every stored time step, which can be slow for long series.
- With the ParaView defaults (Above Upper Threshold, UpperThreshold 0) any non-negative value counts as met, so most entries become the first time; always set the threshold.

## pvCurvature

Generated binding of ParaView's Curvature filter: computes per-point Gaussian (ParaView default) or mean curvature of a polygonal surface into the point array Gauss_Curvature or Mean_Curvature. Gaussian curvature is positive on sphere-like and negative on saddle-like regions (units 1/length²); mean curvature (1/length) assumes outward normals. Use the curated curvature (Schemaxis default Mean) for the usual case; this binding defaults to Gaussian.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Volume meshes are rejected; extract the surface first (surface or pvExtractSurface).
- Results are noisy on coarse or poorly shaped triangulations; smooth or refine first.

## pvD3

Parallel repartitioning (distributed data decomposition): builds a k-d tree over the distributed dataset and redistributes cells so each MPI process owns a spatially contiguous, load-balanced region, optionally with ghost-cell layers; output is an unstructured grid. In a serial run it acts almost as a pass-through, but non-composite input is still converted to an unstructured grid. pvRedistributeDataSet is the newer alternative with more output control.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Image, rectilinear and structured grids become explicit unstructured grids, which can need much more memory; ParaView warns about this.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvDecimate

Reduces the triangle count of a triangle surface with vtkDecimatePro, removing vertices in order of least error until TargetReduction (ParaView default 0.9, about 90 % of triangles removed) is reached. By ParaView default PreserveTopology is off, so the surface may be split along feature edges (FeatureAngle 15°) and holes may open to reach the target. Input must be triangles; run triangulate first. decimate is the curated version (Schemaxis defaults 0.5, topology preserved); pvQuadricClustering is faster on very large meshes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The native defaults remove 90 % of triangles and allow holes; set PreserveTopology true and a smaller TargetReduction when the surface must stay closed.
- Only triangles are processed; triangulate general polygons first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvDecimatePolyline

Reduces the points of polylines by repeatedly deleting the interior vertex with the smallest error until TargetReduction (ParaView default 0.9) of the segments is removed or the next deletion would exceed MaximumError. The error comes from DecimationStrategy: distance of a vertex from the line through its neighbours (Decimation Distance Strategy, default), the angle at the vertex, or a custom point array. End points are kept, but closed loops can collapse to one segment. Use it to simplify streamlines, contours or GIS polylines.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Separate two-point line cells have no interior vertices; join them into polylines first with pvTriangleStrips and JoinContiguousSegments.
- Vertices shared by several polylines are treated independently, which can break junctions.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvDeflectNormals

Tilts surface normals by a vector field: each new normal is normalize(N + ScaleFactor × V), where N is the input point normal (or the constant UserNormal) and V the selected point vector. It is a shading effect for visualizing a vector field on a surface (e.g. bump-like lighting from velocity), not a physical quantity.

- Without input point normals ParaView warns and falls back to UserNormal; compute normals first (normals or pvGenerateSurfaceNormals) for curved surfaces.

## pvDescriptiveStatistics

Computes univariate statistics of each selected array: minimum, maximum, mean, raw moments, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis. Assessment expresses each value as its number of standard deviations from the mean (signed or unsigned). Use it for summary statistics of fields over a mesh or table; counts are per point or cell, not weighted by cell size. Output port 0 is the statistical model (a multiblock of tables) and port 1 the input with assessment arrays added; select them with {"node": id, "port": n}.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- On a non-uniform mesh the mean is not a volume average; use integrate and divide by volume for that.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvDisk

Creates a flat annulus (a disk with a central hole) in the x-y plane centred at the origin, as polydata made of quadrilaterals: InnerRadius to OuterRadius, divided into RadialResolution rings and CircumferentialResolution sectors. Use it as an inlet or outlet patch, seed surface or reference geometry. The curated disk operation exposes the same source with Schemaxis defaults.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default InnerRadius is 0.5, so the disk has a hole; set it to 0 for a solid disk.
- Position and orientation are fixed (x-y plane at the origin); move it with a transform.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvDistributePoints

Redistributes the points of a point set across MPI processes into spatially contiguous regions with roughly equal point counts, by recursively splitting the points in two (a k-d tree). Output is polydata containing the points and their point data but no cells; input cells are ignored. Use it in MPI runs to balance particle or point-cloud data before point-based processing.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The output has no cells, so it is not drawn and cell-based filters see nothing.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvElevation

Adds a floating-point point array named Elevation by projecting each point onto the segment from LowPoint to HighPoint and mapping its position linearly into ScalarRange: the LowPoint end gets the first value, the HighPoint end the second, and points beyond either end are clamped. Use it for height colouring, a linear test ramp or a coordinate along any direction; elevation is the curated version and pvCellGridElevation works on cell grids.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Points beyond the segment all receive the end values; extend LowPoint and HighPoint over the data if the full variation is wanted.
- LowPoint and HighPoint may receive input-dependent ParaView defaults; set them explicitly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvEllipse

Creates an elliptical arc or full ellipse as a polyline: centred at Center, in the plane normal to Normal, with major radius given by the length of MajorRadiusVector and minor radius Ratio × major. - MajorRadiusVector must not be parallel to Normal; VTK then reports an error and produces nothing.

## pvEnSightReader

Reads an EnSight 6 or EnSight Gold case (.case, ASCII or binary), a post-processing format exported by many CFD and structural solvers (OpenFOAM's foamToEnsight among them). Output is a multiblock dataset with one block per EnSight part, carrying the node (point) and element (cell) variables selected in PointArrays and CellArrays; transient cases expose their time steps. ## pvEqualizerFilter

Applies a frequency-domain equalizer to signal columns of a table: each column is Fourier transformed, its spectrum multiplied by a piecewise-linear gain curve given in EqualizerPoints, and transformed back. - Rows are assumed to be equally spaced samples at SamplingFrequencyHz; irregular time steps give a wrong frequency axis.

## pvEvenlySpacedStreamlines2D

Fills a 2-D vector field with streamlines at roughly uniform spacing (Jobard–Lefer algorithm): starting at StartPosition it integrates forward and backward, seeds new lines SeparatingDistance beside existing ones, and stops a line when it comes closer than SeparatingDistance × SeparatingDistanceRatio to another, closes a loop, leaves the domain, slows below TerminalSpeed or reaches MaximumSteps. Input must lie in the x-y plane with in-plane point vectors; output is polylines with IntegrationTime, interpolated fields and a ReasonForTermination cell array. Use it for even flow pictures of 2-D slices; streamTracer seeds from a chosen source.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- A slice not lying in the x-y plane gives wrong or no streamlines; transform it into x-y first.
- With the default Cell Length unit, distances are multiples of the diagonal of the cell containing StartPosition, so moving the seed rescales all spacings; choose Length for dataset units.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `EvenlySpacedStreamlines2D`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvExodusIIReader

Reads Exodus II finite-element results (.e, .exo, .g, .ex2 …, written by SEACAS-based codes such as Sierra, MOOSE or Cubit) into a multiblock dataset of unstructured grids: element blocks, optional face and edge blocks, node, side and element sets, and global variables, with nodal and element result variables per time step. By default node positions include the displacement vector (ApplyDisplacements, scaled by DisplacementMagnitude). Use pvRestartedSimExodusReader for a restarted run described by a metadata file, or pvIOSSReader, the IOSS-based alternative.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- FilePattern, FilePrefix and XMLFileName are optional, as their ParaView file lists are marked optional. Leave them out to read FileName as given: FilePattern and FilePrefix rebuild the file name from a printf-style pattern, so supplying them changes which file is read, and XMLFileName names an optional part and material description.
- VTK's Exodus reader starts with every result variable disabled; list the PointVariables and ElementVariables you need, or the blocks arrive without fields.
- Coordinates are deformed by default; set ApplyDisplacements to false to see the undeformed mesh.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `ExodusIIReader`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

Coverage: `{"defaults":"native defaults for omitted options","gaps":{},"origin":"generated","output":"native inspection required; explicit output-port selection available","outputPorts":null,"qualification":"not-run"}`.

## pvExtractAMRBlocks

Extracts chosen datasets (boxes) from an AMR input (vtkUniformGridAMR), each identified by its refinement level and its index within that level. The output is a multiblock with one block per level, each holding the extracted uniform grids as pieces. Use it to inspect or process individual AMR patches; pvConvertAMRdatasettoMultiblock or pvResampleAMR convert the whole hierarchy instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- SelectedDataSets is a flat list of (level, index) pairs; Schemaxis rejects an odd number of entries.
- Indices restart at 0 on every level; they are not global block numbers.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractAttributes

Converts one attribute association of the input (points, cells, field data, vertices, edges or rows) into a table (vtkTable): one column per array, one row per point or cell (or other element). Composite input gives a multiblock of tables. Use it to inspect or export raw array values, e.g. as CSV through a table writer. Geometry and connectivity are dropped unless AddMetaData adds coordinates.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default association is Points; set FieldAssociation to Cells for cell-centred solver fields.
- Point coordinates are not included by default; enable AddMetaData when you need them.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractBlock

Full native Extract Block: keeps selected blocks of a multiblock, partitioned dataset collection or AMR input, chosen by Selectors (path expressions) evaluated against the data assembly named in Assembly — the block hierarchy, or an assembly supplied by readers such as IOSS or CGNS that groups blocks by meaning. The composite type is kept (overlapping AMR becomes a partitioned dataset collection). Use extractBlock when the hierarchy is enough.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Selectors must match the chosen assembly; a hierarchy path does not select anything in a reader-defined assembly.
- Without selectors no block is selected and the output is empty.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractCTHParts

Specialized for CTH shock-physics results: for each selected cell-centred volume-fraction array (VolumeArrays) it converts the array to point data and contours it at VolumeFractionValue (ParaView default 0.45), giving one material surface per array. Output is a multiblock with one polydata block per selected array, optionally clipped by a plane (ClipType, ParaView default None) and capped to look closed. Input is CTH data: non-overlapping AMR or multiblock rectilinear grids with cell data, e.g. from pvSpyPlotReader.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- VolumeArrays has no static default; list the material volume-fraction arrays explicitly.
- The surface level is VolumeFractionValue (0.45 by default, not the 0.5 stated in the upstream description); keep the same value when comparing runs.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `ExtractCTHParts`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvExtractCellsAlongLine

Extracts every cell of the input that the straight segment from Point1 to Point2 intersects and outputs those cells, with their point and cell data, as an unstructured grid. Use it to inspect the actual mesh cells crossed by a probe line, for example before plotting with probeLine; probeLine instead samples interpolated values at evenly spaced points. Use pvExtractCellsAlongLinesCustomSource for polylines or several lines.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Cells that only touch the line at a point or edge may or may not be counted; extend the segment slightly if boundary cells matter.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractCellsByRegion

Extracts the cells lying entirely inside (ParaView default) or entirely outside an implicit region — a Plane (ParaView's default choice, whose inside is the side opposite its normal), Box or Sphere — without cutting them, and outputs an unstructured grid. Extractintersected adds cells straddling the region boundary and Extractonlyintersected keeps only those. Use it to cut out a sub-volume of whole original cells; clip cuts cells exactly at the surface and slice returns the surface itself.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The cut is jagged because whole cells are kept; use clip for an exact boundary.
- For a Plane, inside is the negative side, opposite to the normal; flip the normal or choose outside to keep the other half.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractEnclosedPoints

Keeps the input points that lie inside a closed, manifold polygonal Surface (second input) and outputs them as a point cloud (polydata) on port 0; with GenerateOutliers, port 1 holds the points outside. Only points and their point data are kept, not the input's cells. Use it to select particles or probe points within a body; to keep mesh cells, use a clip instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With an open or non-manifold surface the inside/outside test is undefined; enable CheckSurface so the filter first checks that the surface is closed. If that check fails the filter reports "Bad enclosing surface" and stops without producing output (the node fails); it does not mark the points as outside.
- Surface must be a single polygonal surface (not composite); extract the surface of a solid mesh first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvExtractParticlesOverTime

Finds the particles of a temporal point dataset (Particles port) that pass through a volume (Volume port, a dataset with 3-D cells) at any time step, and outputs the Particles data restricted to those particles, still time-dependent. It visits every input time step, so it can be slow. Particles are matched between steps by IdChannelArray. Use it to isolate particles crossing a region such as an inlet or a reaction zone; pvExtractCellsByRegion selects by position at one time only.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- If point order changes between steps and no id array identifies particles, different particles are confused; name an id array in IdChannelArray.
- The Volume must contain 3-D cells; a closed surface does not count as a volume here.

## pvExtractRegionSurface

Extracts polygonal surfaces of an unstructured grid on its outer boundary and also on internal interfaces between regions, where regions are defined by an integer cell array (RegionArrayName, ParaView default "material"). It suits multi-material meshes: each interface face is output once or once per side (SingleSided), and output faces can record their source cell (OrigCellIds) and the face of that cell (CellFaceIds). Use surface or pvExtractSurface when only the outer boundary is needed.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The region array must be an integer (vtkIntArray) cell array; an array of another type, or a name that does not exist, is not used, and only the outer surface results.
- Interfaces are found for unstructured-grid input; other dataset types get the ordinary outer surface.

## pvExtractTimeSteps

Restricts a time-varying input to selected time steps, given as listed zero-based indices (Select Time Steps, ParaView default) or as an inclusive index range with a stride (Select Time Range). Downstream nodes see only those steps: a request for an unselected time is answered by a selected step chosen by ApproximationMode (Nearest Time Step by default), and times outside the selection get the first or last selected step. Use it to thin a long transient before temporalStatistics or pvParticlePath, or to hold a branch at one step.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Indices are positions in the input's time list, not time values; indices beyond the last step are ignored without warning.

## pvFDSReader

Reads Fire Dynamics Simulator results through the Smokeview .smv file, which lists the other output files. The output is a partitioned dataset collection with five groups: Grids (meshes), Devices (point measurements over time), HRR (heat-release-rate tables), Slices and Boundaries (field data on planes and walls). AssemblySelectors chooses which of these are read. Use it for fire and smoke CFD from NIST FDS.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Neither ParaView 5.13.3 nor vtkFDSReader defines default selectors, so an empty selection appears to read nothing; set AssemblySelectors explicitly, e.g. ["/"] for everything.
- Keep the .smv file in the same folder as the files it lists; their paths are resolved relative to it.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvFFTOfSelectionOverTime

ParaView's compound filter that extracts the values of selected points or cells over all time steps (as Plot Selection Over Time does) and applies a discrete Fourier transform to each resulting time series (Table FFT), producing tables for spectral plots. Connect Input to the temporal dataset and Selection to a selection-source node (e.g. pvIDSelectionSource or pvLocationSelectionSource). Use it to find dominant frequencies of probe signals such as vortex shedding; use pvPlotSelectionOverTime and pvTableFFT separately when you need the frequency column or windowing.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The compound definition disables the frequency column and uses a rectangular window and a two-sided spectrum, so rows are frequency bins without frequency labels.
- Every time step of the input is executed; long series are slow, and uneven time spacing invalidates the FFT assumption of constant sampling.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `FFTOfSelectionOverTime`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvFidesJSONReader

Reads ADIOS2 data through Fides using an explicit Fides data model given as a JSON file, which describes how ADIOS2 variables form coordinates, cells and fields. The data model names one or more data sources, and DataSourcePath tells the reader which BP file or stream each source is. The output is a partitioned dataset collection. ParaView marks this route as mainly for debugging data models; use pvFidesReader when the BP output carries its own Fides metadata.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Without a DataSourcePath for each source named in the JSON model nothing can be read; give the source name exactly as in the JSON.
- ParaView's DataSourceIO is not exposed: it takes the memory address of a live ADIOS2 object, which Fides dereferences.

## pvFiniteElementFieldDistributor

Turns element-wise finite-element coefficients into point fields for visualization: it duplicates points so each element owns its own nodes, promotes cells to higher-order Lagrange types where needed, and evaluates H(Grad) discontinuous-Galerkin scalars and H(Curl)/H(Div) vector fields at those nodes. Input must be a partitioned dataset collection whose field data has an "Information Records" string array describing bases and fields (Intrepid2 conventions, e.g. Exodus files read with the IOSS reader); the output has the same structure with the distributed point arrays.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Without a valid Information Records array the filter fails; ordinary meshes are not suitable.
- Pyramid elements are not supported, and the duplicated points make the output larger than the input.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvFlashReader

Reads output of the FLASH astrophysics code (HDF5 plot or checkpoint files) into an overlapping AMR (hierarchical box) dataset: nested refinement levels of uniform blocks with cell-centred variables. Level sets the finest level loaded, counted from the root level 0 (ParaView default 1), and every variable starts disabled, so name the ones you need in CellArrayStatus. Several files form a time series. For particles use pvFLASHAMRParticlesReader; to analyse on a uniform grid, follow with pvResampleToImage or pvResampleAMR.

- The native help text says this reader loads 'Enzo format'; that is a copy error in the ParaView XML. It reads FLASH files; use pvEnzoReader for Enzo.
- Level 1 shows only the two coarsest levels; raise it (up to the file's level count) before measuring fine-scale features, accepting more memory.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvForceStaticMesh

Caches the geometry and topology of its input the first time it runs and keeps reusing that mesh for later time steps, updating only point, cell and field data while the point and cell counts stay the same. Use it after readers or filters that rebuild an unchanged mesh at every time step, so that downstream work depending only on the mesh need not be repeated. It handles an unstructured grid, polydata, or the first block of a composite input when that block is an unstructured grid.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- If the mesh really moves or is remeshed with the same counts, the cached geometry is wrong, and ParaView 5.13.3 offers no way to force the cache to recompute: ForceCacheComputation has no elements, so invoking it sends no message, and assigning it pushes the XML command SetCacheComputation, which vtkForceStaticMesh lacks (it has SetForceCacheComputation) and which aborts the native process. Schemaxis therefore does not expose it. Use a different filter chain for meshes that change.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `ForceStaticMesh`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvForceTime

Makes its output use one fixed time, ForcedTime (ParaView default 0.0), whatever time the scene requests: the upstream pipeline is updated once at ForcedTime, the result is cached, and every time step it reports is replaced by ForcedTime. Use it to hold a reference state, such as the initial geometry or a chosen snapshot, fixed while the rest of the scene follows the selected times. With IgnorePipelineTime false it passes the input through unchanged.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ForcedTime is a time value in the input's units, not an index; use a stored time, because how a time between stored steps is served is decided by the upstream reader.
- ParaView's static ForcedTime is 0.0; set it explicitly when the case does not start at 0.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `ForceTime`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvFrustumSelectionSource

Creates a frustum selection: everything inside a convex volume bounded by six planes, given by the eight corner vertices in Frustum. This is how ParaView stores a rubber-band selection through a camera view, but any convex hexahedral region (e.g. a box) can be described. The output is a vtkSelection (no geometry) for the Selection port of pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. For an axis-aligned box clip, pvClip with a Box type is often simpler.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Corner order matters: swapping near and far faces turns the planes inside out and selects nothing.
- FieldType defaults to CELL; set POINT when the IDs or values refer to points, otherwise the wrong elements are matched.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGDALRasterReader

Reads a GIS raster (GeoTIFF, DEM, ERDAS and the other formats supported by GDAL) into a uniform grid (vtkUniformGrid, supporting blanking of no-data pixels) whose bands are cell-data arrays, one cell per raster pixel. Colour bands are by default collated into one RGB, RGBA, grey-alpha or palette array. Use it for terrain heights, satellite images or land-use maps; warp a height band with warpScalar to obtain terrain.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Band values are cell data; run cellToPoint before operations that need point data, such as warping by a height band.
- Coordinates are in the raster's projection units; nothing is reprojected.

## pvGaussianResampling

Splats the input points into a uniform volume (vtkImageData, point array SplatterValues): each point adds a Gaussian kernel ScaleFactor × value × exp(ExponentFactor × r² / R²) to nearby voxels within radius R, and overlapping contributions are combined by the accumulation mode (ParaView default Max). Without a selected array, or with scale splats off, each point contributes the kernel alone, giving a smooth point-density field. Use it to turn scattered particles or measurements into a continuous field for contouring or volume rendering; use pvResampleToImage to sample an existing mesh instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The default 50 × 50 × 50 grid can be too coarse or too costly; choose ResamplingGrid deliberately, because time grows with the voxel count.
- Fill Volume Boundary (on by default) overwrites the outer layer of voxels with Fill Value, which can create artificial contours at the box faces.
- Points cannot splat into other processes' regions, so MPI results can differ near partition boundaries. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `GaussianResampling`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `EllipiticalEccentricity` | Control the shape of elliptical splatting. Eccentricity is the ratio of the major axis (aligned along normal) to the minor (axes) aligned along other two axes. So Eccentricity gt 1 creates needles with the long axis in the direction of the normal; Eccentricity lt 1 creates pancakes perpendicular to the normal vector. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `EllipticalSplats` | Turn on/off the generation of elliptical splats. If normal warping is on, then the input normals affect the distribution of the splat. This boolean is used in combination with the Eccentricity ivar. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `EmptyCellValue` | Set the Null value for output points not receiving a contribution from the input points. (This is the initial value of the voxel samples.) | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `ExtenttoResample` | Set / get the (xmin,xmax, ymin,ymax, zmin,zmax) bounding box in which the sampling is performed. If any of the (min,max) bounds values are min >= max, then the bounds will be computed automatically from the input data. Otherwise, the user-specified bounds will be used. | `{"items":{"type":"number"},"maxItems":6,"minItems":6,"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `FillValue` | Specify the cap value to use. (This instance variable only has effect if the ivar Capping is on.) | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `FillVolumeBoundary` | Turn on/off the capping of the outer boundary of the volume to a specified cap value. This can be used to close surfaces (after isosurfacing) and create other effects. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `GaussianExponentFactor` | Set / get the sharpness of decay of the splats. This is the exponent constant in the Gaussian equation. Normally this is a negative value. | `{"maximum":0.0,"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `GaussianSplatRadius` | Radius of influence of each splat as a fraction of the longest side of the sampling box: 0.1 means 10 % of that length. Voxels farther away receive nothing; larger values give smoother, more overlapping fields and longer run times. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `ResampleField` | Choose a scalar array to splat into the output cells. If ignore arrays is chosen, point density will be counted instead. | `{"items":{"type":"string"},"maxItems":2,"minItems":2,"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `ResamplingGrid` | Set / get the dimensions of the sampling structured point set. Higher values produce better results but are much slower. | `{"items":{"type":"integer"},"maxItems":3,"minItems":3,"type":"array"}` | omitted |

## pvGenerateQuadraturePoints

Creates a point cloud (polydata with one vertex per quadrature point) from the selected quadrature offset array, carrying as point data the field-data arrays previously interpolated to the same offsets. The quadrature tools work in sequence: pvGenerateQuadratureSchemeDictionary adds a cell offset array QuadratureOffset carrying the quadrature rules, pvInterpolatetoQuadraturePoints evaluates point fields at the quadrature points, and pvGenerateQuadraturePoints turns them into a point cloud. Use it to view or export quadrature-point values, e.g. for finite-element verification.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only field arrays linked to the selected offset array are carried; run pvInterpolatetoQuadraturePoints with the same offset array first.
- A missing dictionary yields an empty output with only a logged error.

## pvGenerateQuadratureSchemeDictionary

Adds a cell array QuadratureOffset (one offset per cell) whose metadata holds a quadrature-rule dictionary for each cell type, the starting point of ParaView's quadrature workflow. Rules exist only for triangles, quadratic triangles, pixels, quads, quadratic quads, tetrahedra and quadratic tetrahedra.

## pvGenerateTimeSteps

Passes its input through unchanged (shallow copy) but declares a new list of time steps (TimeStepValues), ignoring any time steps the input reports. Use it to give static or untimed data a time axis, so temporal filters or time-dependent scenes downstream have steps to work with. It only relabels: a request for one of the new times is passed upstream unchanged, so static input returns the same data at every step and nothing is interpolated.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- To create intermediate states of genuinely transient data use pvTemporalInterpolator instead.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `GenerateTimeSteps`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvGenericIOMultiBlockReader

Reads HACC GenericIO particle files (.gio) into a multiblock dataset with one unstructured-grid block per block stored in the file (usually one per writing MPI rank), vtkPGenericIOMultiBlockReader. Coordinate, array and halo settings work as in pvGenericIOReader. Choose it to keep the file's decomposition, for example to read back pvWriteGenericIOWriter output; use pvGenericIOReader for a single particle grid.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The underlying reader class defaults the coordinate names to x, y and z, but ParaView may replace them from the file; set xAxis, yAxis and zAxis explicitly.
- ParaView marks the GenericIO readers mpi_required; Schemaxis's serial writer fixture read a GenericIO file successfully with pvGenericIOMultiBlockReader, but other files are unverified.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGenericIOReader

Reads HACC GenericIO particle files (.gio) into one unstructured grid of particles (vtkPGenericIOReader): xAxis, yAxis and zAxis name the coordinate variables, PointArrayStatus chooses the other variables to load, and HalosToLoad with HaloId can restrict reading to particles of chosen halos. Several file names form a time series. Its output suits pvANLHaloFinder; use pvGenericIOMultiBlockReader to keep the file's blocks separate and pvMultiResGenericIO for multi-resolution .gios sets.

- Set xAxis, yAxis and zAxis; without valid coordinate variables no points are produced.

## pvGeometryFilter

ParaView's rendering geometry extractor (vtkPVGeometryFilter): converts any dataset, including composite and nonlinear-cell data, into polydata of its outer surface or, with UseOutline, its bounding outline, adding original cell and point id arrays by default. Representations use it internally; as a pipeline node it is a robust way to get the renderable surface. For an ordinary surface use surface or pvExtractSurface.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Interior faces are not produced; slice or clip first to see inside a volume.
- Higher NonlinearSubdivisionLevel values multiply the polygon count exponentially.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGhostCells

Generates ghost cells and points: layers of neighbouring cells copied from adjacent blocks of a partitioned dataset or from other MPI processes, marked with vtkGhostType. Supported block types are image, rectilinear, structured, polydata and unstructured grids (and hyper tree grids). Use it before filters that need neighbour information across partition boundaries, such as gradients or smoothing, so results do not show seams; remove the layers afterwards with pvRemoveGhostInformation.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Ghosts are exchanged only between partitions of the same partitioned dataset, not between different datasets of a collection.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI or client-server behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGlobalIDSelectionSource

Creates a selection by global ID: the elements whose value in the input's designated global-ID array (point or cell, per FieldType) equals one of GlobalIDs. Global IDs stay the same across MPI decompositions and across composite blocks, so this is the robust way to pick the same nodes or elements in a partitioned mesh. The output is a vtkSelection (no geometry) for the Selection port of pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. Use pvIDSelectionSource for plain zero-based indices.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The input must carry a global-ID attribute array (e.g. written by the solver, or generated with pvGlobalPointAndCellIds); an ordinary integer array named "GlobalIds" that is not flagged as global IDs is not used.
- FieldType defaults to CELL; set POINT when the IDs or values refer to points, otherwise the wrong elements are matched.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGlobalPointAndCellIds

Assigns global point and cell ids that are unique across all blocks and MPI processes, giving the same id to points duplicated at block or process boundaries (matched within Tolerance) and marking the duplicates as ghost points. Hyper tree grids get cell ids only. Use it before operations that need consistent ids across partitions, such as ghost generation or merging; for simple local indices use generateIds or pvPointAndCellIds.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With Tolerance 0, points must coincide exactly; meshes written with rounding need a small positive tolerance.

## pvGlyph

Places a copy of a glyph shape (arrow, cone, cube, cylinder, line, sphere or 2-D glyph, GlyphType) at points of the input, or at cell centres when the chosen arrays are cell data, oriented by a vector array and scaled by a scalar or vector array; output is polydata. Use it for velocity arrows or sized markers. Use pvGlyphWithCustomSource to glyph with your own geometry.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- By ParaView default only up to 5000 points are glyphed (Uniform Spatial Distribution); choose All Points or Every Nth Point when every point must appear.
- OrientationArray and ScaleArray must have the same association; a point/cell mismatch makes the native filter warn and produce no glyphs.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGlyphWithCustomSource

Like pvGlyph, but the glyph geometry is any polydata connected to the GlyphSource input (e.g. a CAD part or a custom marker), placed at points or cell centres, oriented by a vector array and scaled by a scalar or vector array; output is polydata. Use it when the built-in shapes are not enough.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- By ParaView default only up to 5000 points are glyphed (Uniform Spatial Distribution); choose All Points or Every Nth Point when every point must appear.
- OrientationArray and ScaleArray must have the same association; a point/cell mismatch makes the native filter warn and produce no glyphs.
- The glyph geometry is used in its own coordinates: an arrow-like source should point along +x and be centred where it should attach.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvGradient

Full native Gradient: estimates the gradient of a point or cell array (3 components for a scalar, 9 for a vector), optionally with divergence, vorticity and Q-criterion, and adds them as arrays on the same mesh. Extra settings cover result names, boundary treatment and dimensionality for image data, which neighbouring cells contribute, the value used where no gradient can be computed, a faster approximation, and hyper-tree-grid modes. Use gradient for the common case.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Divergence, vorticity and Q-criterion need a 3-component input array.
- ParaView fills points where the gradient cannot be computed with NaN by default (ReplacementValueOption); such NaNs propagate into later integrals.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `Gradient`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

'Smoothed' uses central differencing by duplicating the boundary values to compute the gradient on the boundary elements (corresponds to the old 'Gradient' filter). 'Non-Smoothed' uses forward/backward differencing with the values of a boundary element and its neighbor to compute the gradient (corresponds to the old 'Gradient Of Unstructured DataSet' filter). | `{"type":"enum","values":["Smoothed","Non-Smoothed"]}` | omitted |

## pvGradientMagnitude

Computes the magnitude of the spatial gradient of an image's point scalars with central differences that account for the pixel spacing, giving image data of the same size (edge values use one-sided neighbours). It is the classic edge-strength image, useful to locate interfaces or fronts. Dimensionality decides whether the z derivative is included. For gradients of general meshes, or vector results, use gradient.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The output has the input's scalar type, so an integer image gives a truncated integer magnitude; convert to float first when precision matters.
- Multi-component scalars are differentiated per component, not combined.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `GradientMagnitude`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvGroupDatasets

## pvGroupTimeSteps

Loads every time step of the input and returns them together as one dataset without time: a multiblock if the input is multiblock, otherwise a partitioned dataset collection, with one block per step named timestep0, timestep1, … (zero-based step index, not the time value). Use it to overlay or export all steps at once, e.g. to compare particle positions.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Every step is held in memory at once; avoid it on long series of large meshes.

## pvH5PartReader

Coordinates come from three scalar arrays chosen by Xarray, Yarray and Zarray (by default the first of x, coords_0, coords0 and so on that exists).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- If the coordinate arrays are not called x/y/z or coords_0/1/2, set Xarray, Yarray and Zarray, or every particle is placed incorrectly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvHierarchicalDataIDSelectionSource

## pvHierarchicalFractal

Test source that builds a refined hierarchy of uniform (or rectilinear) grid blocks around a Mandelbrot-set fractal, with a cell array scaled to look like a material volume fraction (0.5 at FractalValue). It produces a composite, AMR-like dataset and exists to exercise AMR, ghost-level and material-interface filters, not to represent physical data. - The output type differs with RectilinearGrids (hierarchical box versus multiblock, per the VTK class notes); check it before connecting type-specific filters.

## pvHistogram

Bins one component (or the magnitude) of one array into equal-width bins and outputs a table with bin_extents (bin centre positions) and bin_values (counts), plus per-bin averages of the other arrays when CalculateAverages is on. Use it to study a value distribution, e.g. of pressure or velocity magnitude over a mesh. Counts are per point or per cell, not weighted by cell size. Use pvHistogram2D for the joint distribution of two variables.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- On a non-uniform mesh, unweighted counts do not represent volume or area fractions.
- With custom bin ranges, values outside the range are clamped into the first or last bin, not discarded.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvHistogram2D

Builds a joint (2-D) histogram of two array components and outputs it as a 2-D image (vtkImageData) whose point scalars are the counts: X-variable bins along the image x axis, Y bins along y. By ParaView default the Y variable is the gradient magnitude of the X array, the value-versus-gradient plot used to design volume-rendering transfer functions; turn UseGradientasYAxisArray off to histogram two arbitrary arrays, e.g. temperature against pressure. Both arrays must have the same association and number of tuples. Use pvHistogram for one variable.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Origin and spacing only place the image; binning always spans the arrays' finite ranges or the custom ranges. With the defaults (origin [0, 0], spacing [1, 1]) image coordinates are bin indices; enable HistogramBoundsfromInput to read the axes in data units.
- While UseGradientasYAxisArray is true (the native default), InputArrayforYAxis and the Y custom range are ignored.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvHyperTreeGrid

Builds a hyper tree grid (vtkHyperTreeGrid), a tree-based AMR structure: a rectilinear grid of root cells, each refined recursively by a binary (BranchFactor 2) or ternary (3) subdivision described by the Descriptor string. In the descriptor, levels are separated by "|", "R" marks a refined cell and "." a leaf, e.g. "RR | .R. ... | ...". Use it to construct exact test cases for hyper-tree-grid filters; for random trees use pvHyperTreeGridRandom.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The descriptor must be consistent with Dimensions, BranchFactor and MaxDepth (one character per cell on each level); an inconsistent string produces an error or an empty grid.
- Many standard filters do not accept hyper tree grids directly; convert to an unstructured grid first when needed.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvHyperTreeGridAxisReflection

Mirrors a hyper tree grid (vtkHyperTreeGrid, an adaptively refined tree-based grid) across a plane perpendicular to x, y or z: PlaneNormal picks the axis and PlanePosition the plane's coordinate on it. The output holds only the mirrored grid, unlike pvReflect, which can keep the original too, and cell arrays are copied unchanged. For ordinary datasets use reflect or pvReflect.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Omitted, PlaneNormal reads back "X Axis" when the node is created, whatever the XML says (a bounded native probe), so by the source the grid is mirrored about x = PlanePosition (x = 0 unless PlanePosition is set), not about its minimum-x face. Set PlaneNormal to mirror about y or z.
- Vector cell arrays are not flipped; their mirrored component keeps its original sign.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvHyperTreeGridDepthLimiter

Truncates a hyper tree grid at a maximum refinement depth: cells at depth SetDepth become leaves and finer levels are dropped, giving a coarser view of an adaptively refined grid. Depth counts from 0 at the root cells; if it is at least the grid's deepest level, the output equals the input. With a material mask present, ParaView notes that the output extent can be larger than the input's.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's static SetDepth is 0, which keeps only the root (coarsest) cells; set the level you want.
- Truncated cells show the values already stored on coarse cells; run pvHyperTreeGridEvaluateCoarse first if they should summarise their children.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvHyperTreeGridEvaluateCoarse

Recomputes the values stored on refined (coarse) cells of a hyper tree grid from their children, for every cell array, with the chosen Operator: Min, Max, Sum, Average (masked children count as Default), Unmasked Average, Elder Child (the first child's value) or Splatting Average; the Don't change options leave coarse values as they are. Leaf values are unchanged. Use it before coarse-level views such as pvHyperTreeGridDepthLimiter so coarse cells summarise their children.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's initial Operator is Don't change fast, which does nothing; choose an operator explicitly.
- Sum and Average are not size-weighted in any physical unit; they combine child values directly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvHyperTreeGridRandom

Builds a hyper tree grid (vtkHyperTreeGrid) with pseudo-random binary refinement: each node is split with probability SplitFraction down to MaxDepth, a target MaskedFraction of cells is masked, and the root grid spans OutputBounds. A "Depth" cell array records each cell's level. The same Seed reproduces the same tree. Use it to stress-test hyper-tree-grid filters; use pvHyperTreeGrid for an exactly specified tree.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Cell counts grow quickly with MaxDepth and SplitFraction; start with small values.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvIGESReader

Reads a IGES CAD file through OpenCASCADE and tessellates its B-rep faces into triangles, giving a multiblock dataset with one polydata block per shape (named from the file, or Unnamed) and a per-cell Colors array from the CAD colours. LinearDeflection and AngularDeflection set how closely the triangles follow curved surfaces; ReadWire adds edges as polylines. Use it to bring CAD geometry in for rendering, clipping or probing; use pvSTEPReader for .step/.stp, and readSTL or pvSTLReader for already-tessellated STL.

- VTK applies no unit conversion; compare the output bounds with the simulation's length unit before combining them.

## pvIOSSReader

Reads Exodus II and CGNS databases through Sandia's IOSS library into a partitioned dataset collection: one partitioned dataset per selected block or set, organized in an assembly by entity type. Spatially partitioned files (name.e.N.r) and restart series (name.e-s.001…) are found automatically. By default all blocks and all fields are read and sets are not. Choose it for finite-element results from Sierra, MOOSE or other Exodus writers; pvExodusIIReader is the older Exodus reader and pvCGNSSeriesReader handles CGNS files IOSS cannot open.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Sets (node, side, element sets) are off by default; list them in NodeSets or SideSets to see boundary groups.
- Nodal displacements are applied to coordinates by default (ApplyDisplacements); turn it off to see the undeformed mesh.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvImageDataToAMR

Converts a uniform image (vtkImageData, at least 2-D) into an overlapping AMR dataset (vtkOverlappingAMR). The input image is the finest level; coarser levels are generated from it with RefinementRatio between consecutive levels, and the hierarchy is split into at most MaximumNumberofBlocks blocks. No resolution is added. Use it to feed AMR operations such as pvExtractAMRBlocks, pvAMRContour or pvResampleAMR from image data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each image dimension minus one must be divisible by RefinementRatio^(Numberoflevels − 1); e.g. 65 points per axis with ratio 2 allows up to 7 levels. Otherwise the filter fails with "Image cannot be refined".
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvImageDataToUniformGrid

Converts image data (vtkImageData, or composite data whose leaves are images) into a vtkUniformGrid with blanking: a single-component point or cell array marks which points or cells are hidden. Values strictly between -1 and 1 (effectively zero) hide the element and other values keep it; Reverse swaps this. The blanking is written as a vtkGhostType array of hidden points or cells, which rendering and blanking-aware filters skip. Use it to mask solid or invalid regions of a regular grid without changing its structure.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- A value such as 0.5 counts as zero and is hidden; use a mask array of clear 0 and 1 values.
- The array must have exactly one component; vector arrays are rejected.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvImageReader

Reads headerless raw binary voxel files (.raw) into uniform image data. The file carries no metadata, so you describe it: DataExtent (index ranges), DataScalarType, DataByteOrder, NumberOfScalarComponents and FileDimensionality, plus DataSpacing and DataOrigin for world placement. Several files are a time series unless ReadAsImageStack stacks 2-D files as z slices. Use pvNrrdReader or pvMetaFileSeriesReader when a header file exists.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- DataExtent starts as all zeros, which describes a single voxel; always set it, e.g. [0, 255, 0, 255, 0, 99] for 256 x 256 x 100 voxels.
- A wrong scalar type or byte order (ParaView defaults: short, BigEndian) still yields an image, only with nonsense values; check the value range after reading.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `ImageReader`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvImageShrink

Reduces the resolution of an image or volume (vtkImageData) by integer factors per axis, either by averaging each block of input pixels (ParaView default) or by keeping every nth pixel. The output spacing grows by the same factors. Use it to make large images manageable for preview or export; use resample or pvResampleToImage for non-integer target resolutions.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Plain subsampling (Averaging false) can alias fine structure; keep averaging for continuous fields.
- Averaging mixes values, so do not use it on label or mask images; switch Averaging off for those.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvInSituParticlePath

Parallel particle-path (pathline) tracer intended for in-situ use, e.g. inside a Catalyst pipeline that advances with a running simulation. Seeds from SeedSource are advected through the time-varying point vector field of Input; it adds options to clear the particle cache, keep advecting from previously computed particles (RestartSource) after a simulation restart, and start at FirstTimeStep. Output is polydata. For post-processing saved time series use pvParticlePath or pvParticleTracer.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Particle paths need the pipeline to step through time; a single update at one time produces only the seeds.
- The vector field must be point data; convert cell vectors with cellToPoint.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI or client-server behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvIntegrateVariables

Integrates every point and cell array over the input cells and sums the total length, area or volume; the output is a single point with one vertex cell holding the results. Only cells of the highest dimension present are used (with lines, triangles and hexahedra mixed, only the hexahedra count) and vertices are ignored. Same native filter as the curated integrate; use it for totals such as a surface-integrated flux or a volume-integrated quantity.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Integrals are not averages: point-data integrals are never divided by the size; divide them yourself (calculator) or use DivideCellDataByVolume for cell data.
- Vectors are integrated component by component; a flux needs a normal-component field on the surface, not the raw velocity.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `IntegrateVariables`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvInterpolatetoQuadraturePoints

Interpolates every point array of the input to the quadrature points of each cell, using the selected quadrature offset array, and stores the results as field-data arrays of the same names (linked to the offset array); the mesh is unchanged. The quadrature tools work in sequence: pvGenerateQuadratureSchemeDictionary adds a cell offset array QuadratureOffset carrying the quadrature rules, pvInterpolatetoQuadraturePoints evaluates point fields at the quadrature points, and pvGenerateQuadraturePoints turns them into a point cloud.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The input needs an offset array with a quadrature dictionary, normally from pvGenerateQuadratureSchemeDictionary; otherwise nothing is computed and ParaView only warns.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvIsoVolume

Keeps the part of the input where a scalar lies between the two bounds of ThresholdRange (inclusive), cutting cells exactly at both iso-values for point arrays; the output is an unstructured grid. Use it for the volume between two levels, e.g. 0.1 < alpha < 0.9 at a phase interface. Unlike threshold, which keeps or drops whole cells, it produces smooth boundaries.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With a cell array, cells are kept or removed whole instead of being cut.
- ParaView's static range is [0, 0], which keeps almost nothing; always set ThresholdRange.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvKMeans

Clusters observations into k groups (ParaView default 5) in the space spanned by the selected arrays, iterating until cluster centres move less than Tolerance or MaxIterations is reached. The model is the set of centres; assessment labels each point or cell with its nearest cluster and the distance to it, e.g. to segment flow regimes. Output port 0 is the statistical model (a multiblock of tables) and port 1 the input with assessment arrays added; select them with {"node": id, "port": n}.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Distances are Euclidean in raw array units, so variables with large magnitudes dominate; normalize them first (calculator).
- Task 3 (Model and assess the same data) assesses data that also trained the model, which flatters the fit; prefer a separate data set via ModelInput.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `KMeans`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvLANLFOFSODHaloFinder

LANL cosmology halo finder (vtkPLANLHaloFinder): it groups particles into friends-of-friends halos using a linking length in units of the interparticle spacing and, if SphereOverdensityHalosSOD is on, also computes spherical-overdensity (SOD) halo mass and radius around each large FOF halo. The input must carry point arrays velocity, mass, tag and ghost, as produced by pvCosmoReader. Port 0 returns the particles with a HaloID array; port 1 one point per halo with HaloMass, AverageVelocity, VelocityDispersion and, with SOD, the SOD arrays.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- GenericIO particle data lack the required velocity, mass, tag and ghost arrays; use pvANLHaloFinder for those.
- Boxsize, Seedparticles and the mass thresholds must match the simulation; defaults are example values.
- MBP and MCP centre finding can be very slow.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvLSDynaReader

Reads an LS-DYNA d3plot database (the d3plot file and its numbered family files d3plot01, d3plot02… holding later states) as a time series. The output is a multiblock dataset with one unstructured-grid block per selected part, named after the part, carrying nodal arrays (e.g. Velocity, Acceleration) and per-element-type cell arrays (e.g. Stress, EffPlastStrn). Use it for crash, forming and impact results; select parts and arrays to limit memory.

- The mesh is deformed only when "Deflected Coordinates" is among PointArrays and DeformedMesh is true; the reader then also adds a Deflection displacement array.

- VTK notes that rigid-body and road-surface support is incomplete.

## pvLegacyParticlePath

Legacy particle-path (pathline) tracer kept for compatibility with older ParaView states: it integrates particles from the SeedSource points through a time-dependent, point-centred velocity field and outputs polydata polylines, one per particle, up to the time at which the node is updated. - The input must provide several time steps; with a single time step there is nothing to integrate.

## pvLinearCellExtrusion

Extrudes every polygon of a polygonal surface independently into a 3-D cell (triangles to wedges, quads to hexahedra, other polygons to polyhedra) by a length equal to a cell scalar times ScaleFactor, along the cell normal or a user vector; the output is an unstructured grid. Use it for 3-D bar maps, e.g. building heights on a footprint map or values drawn as columns on a surface. Use pvLinearExtrusion to sweep the whole surface by one vector.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only polygons are extruded; vertices, lines and triangle strips are discarded.
- The length array must be a single-component cell array.

## pvLinearExtrusion

Sweeps a polygonal dataset along one vector, creating side faces from its edges and, with Capping, copies of the polygons at both ends; output is polydata. Use it to turn a 2-D outline or planar surface into a prism-like solid surface, e.g. a profile into a constant-thickness part. Use pvLinearCellExtrusion for per-cell heights or volume cells.

- The result is a surface, not a volume mesh; mesh it separately if volume cells are needed.
- Capping a closed surface duplicates it rather than building a solid; turning Capping off for a closed surface gives no output.

## pvLoopSubdivision

Refines a triangle surface with Loop's approximating subdivision: each pass splits every triangle into four and repositions points so the surface becomes smooth; point data are interpolated by the same scheme and new triangles inherit their parent's cell data. Use it to smooth coarse triangulated geometry for display. Input must be polydata of triangles only (run triangulate first). Because points move, the result no longer passes through the original vertices; use pvSubdivide for refinement that keeps the shape.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each pass quadruples the triangle count; NumberofSubdivisions 4 gives 256 times as many triangles.
- Do not measure areas or volumes on the smoothed surface as if it were the original geometry.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvMandelbrot

Generates image data whose float point scalar "Iterations" counts the iterations of z → z² + C before |z| exceeds 2 (capped at MaximumNumberofIterations). The 4-D parameter space (C real, C imaginary, X real, X imaginary, where X is the starting z) is sampled from OriginCX over SizeCX, with ProjectionAxes choosing which three parameters map to the image x, y and z axes. Use it as a synthetic image or volume with fine detail for testing.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The native description calls the values unsigned char; VTK produces float values.
- The output's origin and spacing are in Mandelbrot parameter units, not physical coordinates.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

Values less than 2.0 after the specified number of iterations are considered in the fractal set. | `{"maximum":5000,"minimum":1,"type":"integer"}` | omitted |
| `OriginCX` | The four values of this property indicate (in order) the components of C (real and imaginary) and the components of the initial value, X (real and imaginary). | `{"items":{"type":"number"},"maxItems":4,"minItems":4,"type":"array"}` | omitted |

By default, the real component of C (represented by 0) is mapped to the X axis; the imaginary component of C (represented by 1) is mapped to the Y axis; and the real component of X, the initial value (represented by 2) is mapped to the Z axis. The imaginary component of X is represented by 3. All values entered must be between 0 and 3, inclusive. | `{"items":{"maximum":3,"minimum":0,"type":"integer"},"maxItems":3,"minItems":3,"type":"array"}` | omitted |

## pvMaskPoints

Reduces a dataset to a subset of its points, output as polydata points (optionally with vertex cells) carrying the point data. By ParaView default it keeps every OnRatio-th point by point id (2), starting at Offset, until MaximumNumberofPoints (5000) is reached; random modes instead draw a random or spatially uniform sample. Use it to thin points before glyphs (arrows) or for lighter scatter exports.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- In the default striding mode the 5000-point cap is reached after the first 10000 point ids, so a large mesh is sampled only over part of its id range; raise MaximumNumberofPoints or use random sampling.
- Without GenerateVertices (default false) the output has points but no cells, so it is not drawn and cell-based filters see nothing.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvMedian

Replaces each pixel or voxel of an image by the median of the selected array over a rectangular neighbourhood of KernelSize pixels, giving image data of the same size. Unlike a mean filter it removes isolated outliers (salt-and-pepper or shot noise) while keeping sharp edges. Each component is filtered separately. Near the image border the neighbourhood is clipped to the image.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With the ParaView default kernel [1, 1, 1] nothing changes; set e.g. [3, 3, 1] for a 2-D image or [3, 3, 3] for a volume.
- Even kernel sizes are off-centre and average the two middle values; prefer odd sizes.

## pvMergeBlocks

Full native Merge Blocks: appends the leaf datasets of a composite input into one dataset. OutputDataSetType decides the result: Unstructured Grid (ParaView default) merges blocks of any type, Polygonal Mesh merges only polydata blocks and leaves others out. MergePartitionsOnly keeps the block hierarchy and merges only the partitions within each block. Use merge for the common case (merge everything with point merging); use this when you need polydata output, a merge tolerance or partition-only merging.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With Polygonal Mesh output, volume meshes and image blocks are silently omitted; extract their surfaces first if they must be included.
- Tolerance is a fraction of the bounding-box diagonal unless ToleranceIsAbsolute is true.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvMergeTime

Combines several time-dependent inputs into one multiblock dataset (one block per input) whose time steps are the union of the inputs' times, or their intersection with Intersection on, with near-duplicates removed using Tolerance. ## pvMeshQuality

Adds a cell array Quality rating the shape of each cell with a Verdict metric chosen per cell type (triangle, quad, tetrahedron, pyramid, wedge, hexahedron); other cell types get 0. Use it to locate distorted or degenerate cells before a simulation or to explain solver problems. Each metric has its own scale and ideal value (for example Scaled Jacobian is 1 for an ideal element and negative for inverted ones), so read thresholds from the Verdict documentation. ParaView's defaults are Radius Ratio (triangles, tetrahedra), Edge Ratio (quads, wedges), Shape (pyramids) and Maximum Aspect Frobenius (hexahedra). Use pvCellSize or cellSize for cell size.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- On a mixed mesh the single Quality array holds different metrics for different cell types; compare values only within one cell type or choose comparable metrics.
- Higher-order cells are measured by their own definition unless LinearApproximation is enabled, which adds Quality (Linear Approx).
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvMinMax

Computes, for every point and cell array of the input, the componentwise minimum, maximum or sum over all tuples, and outputs a polydata with exactly one point and one vertex cell that carries the results under the original array names. Use it for one-number summaries such as peak temperature. In parallel runs ghost arrays are needed to avoid double counting. For cell-size-weighted totals use integrate; for distributions use pvHistogram.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- SUM adds raw tuple values; it is not an integral and ignores cell sizes.
- Operation must be MIN, MAX or SUM in upper case; any other string makes the native filter report an error and fall back to MIN.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvMinkowskiFilter

Computes Minkowski functionals and shapefinders for each polyhedral cell of a Voronoi tessellation (vtkMinkowskiFilter). It adds cell arrays S (surface area), V (volume, copied from the input's Volumes array), C (integrated mean curvature), X (Euler characteristic), G (genus), T = 3V/S (thickness), B = S/C (breadth), L = C/(4 pi (G + 1)) (length), and planarity P and filamentarity F, which characterize whether a structure is sheet-like or filament-like. Use it on merged Voronoi regions from pvVoronoiMergeConnected.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Every cell must be a polyhedron and the input must have a Volumes cell array; other unstructured grids are not handled by the native code.
- Lengths and areas are in the dataset's coordinate units; no conversion is applied.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `MinkowskiFilter`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvMulticorrelativeStatistics

Computes the mean vector and covariance matrix (with its Cholesky decomposition) of the selected arrays, i.e. a multivariate Gaussian model, and assesses each observation by its squared Mahalanobis distance from the mean, useful for outlier detection across several correlated fields. Use pvPrincipalComponentAnalysis to add eigen-decomposition. Output port 0 is the statistical model (a multiblock of tables) and port 1 the input with assessment arrays added; select them with {"node": id, "port": n}.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The model tables are packed (upper triangle covariance, lower triangle Cholesky); read the operation reference before parsing them.
- Task 3 (Model and assess the same data) assesses data that also trained the model, which flatters the fit; prefer a separate data set via ModelInput.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `MulticorrelativeStatistics`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvNetCDFMPASreader

Reads one MPAS (Model for Prediction Across Scales) NetCDF file on a global unstructured Voronoi mesh and builds its dual grid as an unstructured grid: MPAS cell variables become point data and vertex variables become cell data. By default it shows vertical level 0 on a sphere as ocean data; options give a multilayer view, a lat/lon projection or atmospheric layering. Edge-centred data and regional (planar) domains are not supported, and it is not a parallel reader.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Additional dimensions (vertical level, tracer index) are fixed to one index per dimension; set ExtraDimensionIndices to choose the slice, or ShowMultilayerView to see all levels.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvNetCDFPOPreader

Reads Parallel Ocean Program (POP) NetCDF output into a rectilinear grid. The NetCDF x, y, z order becomes the grid's z, y, x order, and z coordinates are negated so the first level is the highest (depth downwards). Only three-dimensional variables are offered; Stride subsamples the grid. Use pvNetCDFReader for general CF-convention files and pvParallelNetCDFPOPreader for the parallel variant.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Index order is reversed relative to the NetCDF variable; apply Stride in grid (i, j, k) order.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvNetCDFReader

Reads NetCDF files using the CF (and COARDS) conventions into structured VTK data: image data when nothing else is known, or rectilinear or curvilinear grids when CF coordinate metadata describes them; latitude/longitude grids can be shaped as a sphere (SphericalCoordinates). Dimensions chooses which group of variables (those sharing a dimension list) is loaded, and time comes from the CF time coordinate. Use it for climate, weather and ocean gridded data; use pvNetCDFCAMreader, pvNetCDFMPASreader or pvNetCDFPOPreader for those models' specific layouts.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only variables matching the chosen Dimensions are loaded; set Dimensions when the file mixes grids (e.g. 2-D surface and 3-D level variables).
- Fill values stay as numbers unless ReplaceFillValueWithNan is on, which distorts ranges and averages.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

A warning is issued if a mismatch occurs. | `{"type":"enum","values":["Automatic","Image","Rectilinear","Structured","Unstructured"]}` | omitted |
| `ReplaceFillValueWithNan` | If on, any float or double variable read that has a _FillValue attribute will have that fill value replaced with a not-a-number (NaN) value. The advantage of setting these to NaN values is that, if implemented properly by the system and careful math operations are used, they can implicitly be ignored by calculations like finding the range of the values. That said, this option should be used with caution as VTK does not fully support NaN values and therefore odd calculations may occur. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

It is common to write the vertical component with respect to something other than the center of the sphere (for example, the surface). In this case, it might be necessary to scale and/or bias the vertical height. The height will become height*scale + bias. Keep in mind that if the positive attribute of the vertical dimension is down, then the height is negated. The scaling will be adjusted if it results in invalid (negative) vertical values. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `VerticalScale` | The scale of the vertical component of spherical coordinates. ## pvNetCDFUGRIDreader

Reads a NetCDF file that follows the UGRID conventions for unstructured meshes (used by some ocean, coastal and climate models) into an unstructured grid. vtkNetCDFUGRIDReader reads one 2-D mesh: mesh nodes become points and faces become cells (edges are not read), node variables become point arrays and face variables cell arrays, and a "time" variable provides time steps. Use pvNetCDFReader for CF-convention gridded NetCDF, pvNetCDFMPASreader for MPAS meshes or pvNetCDFPOPreader for POP ocean grids.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's long help mentions a separate connectivity file, but ParaView 5.13.3 exposes no such property: the mesh topology and the data must be in the file given in FileName.
- Only one 2-D mesh is read; edge-located variables and additional meshes in the file are not represented.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.
