## pvNetworkImageSource

ParaView-internal source that reads an image file on one process and makes the image available on the client and render-server processes, used for textures and background images. In ReadFromMemory mode it instead fetches an image registered under TrivialProducerKey on the server. It is not a general network download. To read image data for analysis use readImageData or a pv image reader such as pvPNGSeriesReader.

- FileName is required by the Schemaxis binding even in ReadFromMemory mode.

## pvNormalGlyphs

ParaView's compound Normal Glyphs filter: extracts the outer surface, computes one normal per surface cell, and draws an arrow glyph at every cell centre along that normal. The output is polydata of arrows, typically rendered over the surface to check normal orientation, e.g. before extrusion, offsets or boundary-condition assignment. Arrow length is the glyph scale factor in dataset units; all arrows have the same size.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Polygon ordering is used as found (Consistency is off in this filter by default), so mixed-orientation surfaces show arrows pointing both ways; that is often what you want to detect.
- Every surface cell gets an arrow; on large surfaces decimate or extract a region first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `NormalGlyphs`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Consistency` | The value of this property controls whether consistent polygon ordering is enforced. Generally the normals for a data set should either all point inward or all point outward. If the value of this property is 1, then this filter will reorder the points of cells that whose normal vectors are oriented the opposite direction from the rest of those in the data set. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `GlyphMaxPoints` | Native Glyph MaximumNumberOfSamplePoints, which caps the number of glyphs only in the Glyph filter's uniform-spatial-distribution modes. Normal Glyphs fixes its internal glyph mode to All Points, so this value does not limit the arrows here. | `{"type":"integer"}` | omitted |
| `GlyphScaleFactor` | Length of every arrow in dataset coordinate units: the arrow source has unit length and no data array scales it, so this value is the displayed arrow length. Choose a few percent of the model size so arrows are visible without hiding the surface. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `InvertArrow` | Reverses the arrow geometry so each glyph points against the computed normal instead of along it. Use it when the surface normals point into the body and you want arrows outside; the normals themselves are unchanged. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |


## pvNrrdReader

Reads NRRD images (.nrrd, or a detached .nhdr header with its data file or files) into uniform image data, taking dimensions, type and spacing from the header. vtkNrrdReader reads raw, ascii (also spelled txt or text) and gzip-compressed (gzip or gz) data; hex and bzip2 encodings are rejected with 'Unsupported encoding'. ## pvOMETIFFChannelCalculator

Combines up to ten fluorescence-microscopy channels of an OME-TIFF image into one RGBA colour image. Each enabled point array named Channel_1 to Channel_10 (the names pvOMETIFFReader produces) is mapped through its ChannelNLUT lookup table, its opacity is multiplied by ChannelNWeight, and the channels are blended additively into a new unsigned-char point array named Colors; the input image and its arrays are passed through unchanged. Use it to make a false-colour composite for display or PNG export; the channel data themselves are not modified.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Every enabled channel needs a lookup table: an enabled array without a ChannelNLUT stops the filter with "No LUT specified". Connect a pvResourcePVLookupTable to the matching ChannelNLUT input (opacity mapping on) for each channel you enable.
- Lookup tables and weights are keyed by the names Channel_1 to Channel_10; arrays with other names cannot be given a lookup table.
- ParaView's GUI creates default colour maps (blue, green, red, magenta, cyan, grey) when the proxy is initialized with input data available; Schemaxis has not verified that this happens for its nodes, so connect the tables explicitly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvOctreeImagetoPointSet

Reverses pvPointSetToOctreeImage: reads an image whose cell scalars are the unsigned-char "octree" bit mask and emits polydata with one point for every set bit, placed at the centre of the corresponding octant of the cell (a quarter of the spacing from the cell centre). It can also copy one component of a chosen cell array to the generated points. Use it to rebuild an approximate point cloud from a compact octree image; positions are quantized to octants, so original coordinates are not recovered.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The active cell scalars must be the unsigned-char octree mask produced by pvPointSetToOctreeImage (array "octree"); other images give meaningless points.
- pvPointSetToOctreeImage outputs a partitioned dataset holding one image; if this filter rejects it, extract the image block first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvOpenFOAMReader

Full native OpenFOAM reader: opens a case through its .foam marker and outputs a multiblock dataset with the selected mesh regions (internalMesh, patches, patch groups, Lagrangian clouds and optionally zones) carrying cell, point and Lagrangian fields for each stored time. Omitted settings keep ParaView's own defaults: Reconstructed Case, the 0 directory skipped, point data interpolated from cell fields, 32-bit labels and 64-bit scalars. Use the curated foam operation for the common case (decomposed case, internalMesh only, 0 kept); use this one for point or Lagrangian fields, zones, binary label/scalar sizes and the other native options.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- SkipZeroTime is true by ParaView default, so the initial conditions in 0/ are not offered as a time; set it false to inspect them.

## pvOpenVDBReader

Reads an OpenVDB (.vdb) file, the sparse volume format used in visual effects and some simulation tools. Each grid becomes a block of a partitioned dataset collection: volume grids become image data (vtkImageData) and point grids become polydata vertices. MergeImageVolumes or MergePointSets instead combine the selected grids into one image (one array per grid) or one point set, and DownsamplingFactor coarsens the sampled volume.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Sparse volumes are sampled onto a dense image, so a large sparse grid can need much more memory than the file size suggests; try DownsamplingFactor 0.5 for a first look.
- Without merging each grid is a separate block; enable MergeImageVolumes when a later operation needs one image with several arrays.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

## pvOverlappingCellsDetector

Detects cells that overlap other cells of the same mesh and adds a cell array, NumberOfOverlapsPerCell, counting for each cell how many other cells it collides with (the upstream description's name NumberOfCollisionsPerCell is outdated). Use it as a mesh-quality check, e.g. for overlapping overset regions or badly merged parts; zero everywhere means no overlap was found. It accepts point sets and composite data and works across MPI processes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Tolerance is a length: each cell is shrunk by half of it before testing, so contacts within that margin are ignored; too large a value hides genuine overlaps.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPCANormalEstimation

Estimates a normal at every point of a polydata point cloud by principal component analysis: a plane is fitted to each point's neighbours and its normal is stored in the point array PCANormals. Use it for scanned or particle data without connectivity, where surface normals cannot be computed from polygons (use normals or pvGenerateSurfaceNormals for meshed surfaces). The neighbourhood is chosen by SearchMode, SampleSize and Radius; the sign of each normal is arbitrary unless NormalOrientation fixes it.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With the ParaView default orientation As Computed, neighbouring normals can point to opposite sides of the surface; choose Point or Graph Traversal when shading or offsets depend on a consistent side.
- Input must be polydata; convert other datasets with pvConvertToPointCloud first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

With KNN mode K (SampleSize) points are selected regardless of their location relative to the sampled point. The radius can also be set to ensure that a sufficiently large neighborhood is taken into account, if not (i.e. all points fall inside the radius), the second approach is performed. With Radius mode, neighboring points are selected inside a radius (RADIUS), only the neighborhood of the sampled point is considered. If K (SampleSize) is also set, the number of points found inside the radius must be larger than K, if not the first approach is performed. Both approaches give the same results. ## pvPLOT3DReader

Reads NASA PLOT3D structured-grid data: a grid file (.xyz) with block coordinates, solution files (.q) holding density, momentum and stagnation energy, and a function file (.f) of extra variables. The output is a multiblock dataset of structured grids with density, momentum and stagnation energy as point arrays; Functions adds derived quantities (pressure, Mach number, velocity, vorticity …) computed with the reader's gas constants R = 1.0 and γ = 1.4, which are not exposed here. Several .q files form a time series. Use pvPLOT3DMetaFileReader when a .p3d meta file describes the case.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- PLOT3D files are not self-describing: when AutoDetectFormat (ParaView default true) cannot work, e.g. for ASCII files, set BinaryFile, ByteOrder, DoublePrecision, MultiGrid, HasByteCount, IBlanking and TwoDimensionalGeometry to match the writer.
- FunctionFileName and QFileName are optional: leave them out to read the grid file alone. The native reader skips an empty solution or function file name, so a grid-only case is valid and produces no solution arrays.
- Check that R = 1.0 and γ = 1.4 match your solver's normalization before interpreting derived pressure, temperature or Mach number.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

## pvPLYReader

Full native PLY reader: reads Stanford PLY polygon files (ASCII or binary) into polydata. ParaView's documentation requires vertex elements with x, y and z and face elements with vertex_indices; further vertex properties such as normals, colours or texture coordinates are carried along as arrays. Several file names form a time series. Use readPLY for one file; use this operation for file series or the texture-coordinate settings.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- PLY carries no unit; compare the bounds with the simulation's length unit before combining.
- Point-cloud files without face elements fall outside ParaView's documented requirement; check the output before relying on them.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

## pvPNGSeriesReader

Reads PNG images (.png) into uniform image data with 8- or 16-bit, 1 to 4 component point scalars. ## pvParticlePath

Advects particles from the seed points (SeedSource port) through a time-varying vector field (Input port) and outputs pathlines: polylines tracing each particle from injection up to the requested time, with arrays such as ParticleId, ParticleAge and InjectionStepId. It integrates through the input's time steps from the first, so later scene times cost more. Use it for unsteady flows where instantaneous streamlines mislead; pvParticleTracer returns only current positions and streamTracer instantaneous streamlines.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- A single-step input does not move particles; use streamTracer for steady fields.
- TerminationTime is hidden in ParaView 5.13.3 and a no-op in the VTK 9.4.1 source; limit the time span with pvExtractTimeSteps instead.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvParticleTracer

Advects particles from the seed points (SeedSource port) through a time-varying vector field (Input port) and outputs, at the requested time, only the current particle positions as points with attributes such as ParticleId and ParticleAge; no paths are kept and no cells are created. ForceReinjectionEveryNSteps releases new particles periodically for a continuous stream. Use it to animate particle clouds in unsteady flow; pvParticlePath keeps trajectories.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The output has points but no cells, so cell-based operations and surface rendering see nothing; glyph the points or render them as points.
- Each requested time integrates from the first input step, so long transients are slow.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPartitionBalancer

For partitioned data (vtkPartitionedDataSet or collections), makes every MPI process hold the same number of partitions by adding empty (null) partitions, and drops empty input partitions. Squash (ParaView default) pads only up to the largest per-process count; Expand gives every non-empty partition its own global index, so partition n exists on exactly one process. Data and geometry are unchanged. Use it before writers or filters that expect a consistent partition layout; in a serial run it only removes empty partitions.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPedigreeIDSelectionSource

Creates a pedigree-ID selection: elements whose value in the input's designated pedigree-ID array matches the given IDs, which are integers (PedigreeIDs) or strings (PedigreeStringIDs), each paired with a domain name. Pedigree IDs identify where an element came from (e.g. a source-file element number) and survive filtering. ## pvPerlinNoise

Adds a point array (default name PerlinNoise) of deterministic Perlin noise evaluated at each point's coordinates, varying between -|Amplitude| and |Amplitude|; geometry is unchanged. Use it to generate smooth pseudo-random test fields, perturb geometry together with a warp, or add texture for rendering. The same coordinates and settings always give the same values.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Frequency is per unit length of the dataset coordinates; on a domain spanning thousands of units the default 1 gives very fine noise, so scale it to your geometry.

## pvPlane

Creates a flat parallelogram as polydata: Origin is one corner, and the edges run from Origin to Point1 (the plane's x axis) and from Origin to Point2 (its y axis), subdivided into XResolution × YResolution quadrilaterals. Use it as a seed or probe surface, a sampling plane or reference geometry. The curated plane operation offers the same source with Schemaxis defaults.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default resolution is 1 × 1, a single quad; raise the resolution before using it as a probe surface.
- The two edges need not be perpendicular; non-perpendicular edges give a skewed parallelogram.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvPlotDataOverTime

Builds time histories by updating the input at every time step it reports and collecting one attribute association (FieldAssociation: Points by ParaView default, Cells, Vertices, Edges or table Rows). Output is a multiblock of tables with a time column: by default one table of per-step statistics (minimum, maximum, quartiles and, for numeric arrays, mean and standard deviation) per input block, otherwise one table per tracked point or cell. Use it for convergence or transient monitoring of a region already reduced to what matters (a probe, slice or clipped zone).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Every time step is computed, so the cost is the number of steps times the upstream pipeline cost.
- With statistics off, every point or cell becomes its own table; on a large mesh reduce it first (e.g. pvProbeLocation).
- Elements are matched across steps by global ids, else by index; if the mesh changes over time, per-element histories may not follow the same physical location.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPlotOnIntersectionCurves

ParaView's compound filter that extracts the outer surface of the input, cuts it with an implicit function (SliceType, a plane by default) and orders the resulting intersection edges into polylines. The output is a multiblock of polylines carrying the interpolated point data plus an arc_length array, suitable for line plots of a field along the curve, e.g. pressure around an aerofoil section. Use pvPlotOverLine or probeLine to sample along a straight segment through the volume instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only the surface is cut, so the curves show surface values (e.g. wall quantities), not the interior field.
- Separate intersection loops become separate blocks, and their arc length starts at 0 for each.

## pvPlotOverLine

Samples all point and cell arrays of the input along the straight segment Point1-Point2 and returns a polyline (polydata) with the interpolated values plus arc_length and vtkValidPointMask point arrays, ready for line charts or CSV export. SamplingPattern chooses uniform samples (ParaView default, Resolution 1000) or exact cell-boundary or one-per-cell sampling. Composite inputs give a single non-composite line. Use probeLine for the same filter with Schemaxis defaults, and pvResampleToLine for a coarse uniform resampling.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Omitted, Point1 and Point2 are never the static [0, 0, 0]: in a bounded native probe with a polydata upstream a batch run read (1, 1, 1) and (-1, -1, -1), a line unrelated to the data (composite inputs give other uninitialised-bounds corners, by the source), and when the upstream already had data they were the corners of its bounding box. Always set both.
- Samples outside the data have vtkValidPointMask 0 and zero values; filter them out before statistics.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `PlotOverLine`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvPointDatasetInterpolator

Interpolates the point arrays of a point cloud (Input: any point set, e.g. particles, scattered measurements or the points of a mesh) onto the points of a second dataset (Source), weighting nearby cloud points with a kernel. The output keeps Source's type, points and cells and adds the interpolated arrays, so a slice, image or mesh can be coloured by cloud data. Kernels range from Voronoi (nearest point, the ParaView default) to smooth Gaussian or Shepard weighting. Use resample when the data live on a mesh with cells, and pvSPHDatasetInterpolator for SPH particles.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only the Input's points and point arrays are used; its cells and cell data are not interpolated.
- Points with no cloud points inside the kernel footprint receive NullValue (0 by default, NullPointsStrategy "Null Value" per the XML default), which can look like real zeros; choose Mask Points to flag them.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPointDatatoCellData

Converts point arrays to cell arrays by averaging, for each cell, the values at its points; with CategoricalData the most frequent value among the cell's points wins instead, which suits integer labels. The output is the same dataset type with new cell arrays, and by ParaView default the point arrays are dropped. Use it when a step needs cell data, e.g. per-cell statistics or cell-based thresholds; pointToCell is the curated version, and cellToPoint or pvCellDatatoPointData go the other way.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Averaging smooths sharp gradients and is not a conservative transfer of extensive quantities.
- With CategoricalData, a cell whose points carry two equally frequent labels gets one of them deterministically, but VTK's code and its own comment disagree on which (the code's std::max_element keeps the larger value); do not rely on tie order and avoid ties by labelling consistently.
- PassPointData defaults to false here (unlike pointToCell); enable it if later nodes still need the point arrays.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `PointDatatoCellData`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvPointLineInterpolator

Interpolates point data from a point cloud (Input) onto a high-resolution straight line set in the Source options (Point1, Point2, Resolution; ParaView default 1000 intervals), producing a polyline profile for line plots. Use it for profiles through scattered or particle data; for data on a mesh with cells, probeLine samples by cell interpolation instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The line endpoints may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that; their static default is [0, 0, 0] for both, a degenerate line. Set Point1 and Point2 explicitly in dataset coordinates.
- Points with no cloud points inside the kernel footprint receive NullValue (0 by default, NullPointsStrategy "Null Value" per the XML default), which can look like real zeros; choose Mask Points to flag them.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvPointPlaneInterpolator

Interpolates point data from a point cloud (Input) onto a bounded plane set in the Source options (a plane through Center with Normal, limited to BoundingBox plus Padding and refined by Resolution or CellSize), producing a planar grid with interpolated arrays, e.g. a heat-map section through particle or scattered data. - The plane's bounding box may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that (static default [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]); set BoundingBox, Center and Normal explicitly.

## pvPointSetToOctreeImage

Bins a point set (point cloud or any vtkPointSet) into a uniform image covering the points' bounding box, sized so that each cell holds about NumberOfPointsPerCell points. The output (a partitioned dataset containing one image) has an unsigned-char cell array "octree" whose eight bits record which octants of each cell contain points, and optionally a float cell array, named after a chosen single-component point array, with per-cell last value, min, max, count, sum and/or mean components. Use it to voxelize particle or LiDAR data, or with pvOctreeImagetoPointSet as a compact, lossy point-cloud encoding.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- NumberOfPointsPerCell must not exceed the number of input points, otherwise the filter fails.
- With ProcessInputPointArray true, the array must have one component and at least one Compute option must be on; ComputeMean also adds Count and Sum components.
- LastValue is not deterministic under multithreading; prefer Mean, Min or Max for reproducible results.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `PointSetToOctreeImage`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvPointSource

Creates a cloud of NumberOfPoints points placed pseudo-randomly with uniform density inside a sphere of radius Radius around Center, as polydata vertices. Use it as a seed cloud for streamlines or particle tracing, or as test input. With the ParaView defaults (one point, radius 0) it yields a single point at the centre.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Positions come from VTK's pseudo-random generator; do not rely on identical positions across sessions or ParaView versions.
- Radius 0 puts every point at the centre; set a radius when you need a spread.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvPolyLineSource

Creates one polyline through an ordered list of points, optionally closed into a loop. Use it for seed curves, measurement paths, outlines or probe paths that are not straight; for a straight subdivided line use pvLine, for a smooth curve through control points use pvSplineSource.

- Points is a flat list of x, y, z triples; a length that is not a multiple of 3 is rejected.

## pvPrincipalComponentAnalysis

Extends pvMulticorrelativeStatistics with the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (optionally normalized, or robust using medians), and assesses data by projecting each observation onto the principal components, using the full basis, a fixed number of components or enough components to reach a fixed energy fraction. Use it to find dominant correlated modes among several fields or to reduce their dimensionality. Output port 0 is the statistical model (a multiblock of tables) and port 1 the input with assessment arrays added; select them with {"node": id, "port": n}.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Without normalization, variables with large variance dominate the components; choose Normalize using covariances when units differ.
- Task 3 (Model and assess the same data) assesses data that also trained the model, which flatters the fit; prefer a separate data set via ModelInput.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `PrincipalComponentAnalysis`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| `ModelInput` | one node | no | `data` |

Chosen by the ParaView entry text: "Point Data", "Cell Data", "Vertex Data", "Edge Data", "Row Data" or "Field Data". ParaView offers only the associations the connected input has (for example "Row Data" for a table), so a text it does not offer fails with NATIVE_DOMAIN_MISMATCH when the node is configured. | `{"type":"enum","values":["Point Data","Cell Data","Vertex Data","Edge Data","Row Data","Field Data"]}` | omitted |
| `BasisEnergy` | The minimum energy to use when determining the dimensionality of the new space into which the assessment will project tuples. | `{"maximum":1.0,"minimum":0.0,"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `BasisScheme` | When reporting assessments, should the full eigenvector decomposition be used to project the original vector into the new space (Full basis), or should a fixed subset of the decomposition be used (Fixed-size basis), or should the projection be clipped to preserve at least some fixed "energy" (Fixed-energy basis)?<p> As an example, suppose the variables of interest were {A,B,C,D,E} and that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix for these were {5,2,1.5,1,.5}. If the "Full basis" scheme is used, then all 5 components of the eigenvectors will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple in the original data into a new 5-components space.<p> If the "Fixed-size" scheme is used and the "Basis Size" property is set to 4, then only the first 4 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space and that space will be of dimension 4, not 5.<p> If the "Fixed-energy basis" scheme is used and the "Basis Energy" property is set to 0.8, then only the first 3 eigenvector components will be used to project each {A,B,C,D,E}-tuple into the new space, which will be of dimension 3. The number 3 is chosen because 3 is the lowest N for which the sum of the first N eigenvalues divided by the sum of all eigenvalues is larger than the specified "Basis Energy" (i.e., (5+2+1.5)/10 = 0.85 > 0.8). | `{"type":"enum","values":["Full basis","Fixed-size basis","Fixed-energy basis"]}` | omitted |
| `BasisSize` | The maximum number of eigenvector components to use when projecting into the new space. | `{"minimum":1,"type":"integer"}` | omitted |
| `NormalizationScheme` | Before the eigenvector decomposition of the covariance matrix takes place, you may normalize each (i,j) entry by sqrt( cov(i,i) * cov(j,j) ). ## pvQuadricClustering

Simplifies a polygonal surface by spatial binning: the bounding box is divided into NumberofDimensions bins, all points in a bin collapse to one representative point chosen to minimize quadric error, and degenerate triangles are dropped. It is fast enough for huge meshes (ParaView uses it for level-of-detail rendering), but the result follows the bin grid rather than surface features. Use pvDecimate or decimate when shape fidelity matters more than speed.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Detail smaller than one bin is lost, including thin walls and small holes; increase the divisions on the relevant axis.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `QuadricClustering`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvRTXMLPolyDataReader

Real-time VTK XML polydata reader (vtkRTXMLPolyDataReader): it can watch a data directory (Location, optional) for .vtp files arriving from a running simulation; each run of its UpdateToNextFile command reads the next unprocessed file, and ResetReader rescans the directory. FileName names the polydata file read first. Schemaxis declares both commands for onVisit, but a batch run sees only the files present while it runs; use pvXMLPolyDataReader for a fixed file or series.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The order in which arriving files are taken is decided by the native reader and has not been checked by Schemaxis.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

## pvRectilinearGridConnectivity

Extracts material fragments from rectilinear-grid data (single grids or multiblock collections, typically CTH results) using cell-centred volume-fraction arrays and an isovalue. Fragments are built at sub-cell resolution with an extended marching-cubes table, connected across blocks and MPI processes, and returned as a multiblock dataset with one polydata block per material; cell data carry FragmentId and the integrated attributes such as MaterialVolume. Choose it for fragment counting and volume integration on rectilinear CTH data; for AMR input use pvMaterialInterfaceFilter or pvAMRFragmentsFilter.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Select at least one volume-fraction array; none is selected by default, so the filter produces nothing until you name one.
- All selected volume-fraction arrays must have the same data type; mixing float, double and unsigned-char arrays stops the filter.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI or client-server behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvRectilinearGridGeometryFilter

Converts a rectilinear grid (vtkRectilinearGrid: axis-aligned cells with separate coordinate arrays along x, y and z) into polygonal data. VTK can restrict this to an i-j-k extent, but ParaView exposes no extent, so the whole grid is used: a 3-D grid becomes a cloud of vertices (one per grid point), a 2-D grid a surface of quadrilaterals and a 1-D grid a polyline, with point and cell data carried over. Use surface or pvExtractSurface to get the outer surface of a 3-D grid instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only vtkRectilinearGrid input works: the ParaView domain accepts any dataset, but the VTK class requires a rectilinear grid, so other inputs fail natively.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvRedistributeDataSet

Load-balances a dataset across MPI processes: it computes spatial cuts for the requested number of partitions and moves cells accordingly, assigning boundary cells to one region (ParaView default), duplicating them (marked as duplicate ghost cells) or splitting them. Output is an unstructured grid per process, or a vtkPartitionedDataSet with PreservePartitionsInOutput, and global cell ids can be generated. With default settings a serial run has one partition, so the main effect is conversion to an unstructured grid. It is the newer alternative to pvD3.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Image, rectilinear and structured grids become explicit unstructured grids, which can need much more memory; ParaView warns about this.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvReductionFilter

Generic parallel reduction (vtkReductionFilter): an optional pre-gather algorithm runs on each MPI process, the results are gathered, and a post-gather algorithm combines them on one or all processes. The helpers are named by VTK class name (PreGatherHelperName, PostGatherHelperName); the helper proxies themselves cannot be set in Schemaxis. In a serial run there is a single piece, so the operation mainly applies the helpers to it. Prefer pvAppendReduce for the common gather-and-append case.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- This proxy's ReductionMode labels for values 0 and 1 are swapped relative to VTK's meaning; read the ReductionMode help before choosing.
- Schemaxis serial examples do not establish MPI behaviour. Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvReflect

Mirrors the input across an axis-aligned plane and outputs an unstructured grid containing, by ParaView default, both the original and the mirrored copy (CopyInput). The plane is either a face of the input bounding box (X Min to Z Max) or x, y or z = Center. Vectors, normals and tensors are flipped; with FlipAllInputArrays (default true) every signed 3-, 6- or 9-component array is treated as a vector or tensor too. Use it to complete a symmetric half-model; the curated reflect uses the same filter with Schemaxis defaults (plane X at 0).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default plane is X Min, the minimum-x face of the bounding box, not x = 0; choose X with Center 0 for a symmetry plane at the origin.
- The two halves are not merged, so points on the mirror plane are duplicated; run cleanGrid if connectivity across the plane matters.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvRemoteSourceProxy

ParaView's Remote Source Proxy (vtkPVMultiServerDataSource) mirrors, inside the client's built-in session, a dataset that lives on another server in a multi-server ParaView setup. It has no inputs or file and receives its data only through a native DependencyLink to that external proxy, which Schemaxis does not expose (it is listed as a property gap). In a Schemaxis workflow it therefore has nothing to fetch and is not a useful data source; use a reader or a source operation instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The DependencyLink binding is an unsupported native property class, so the node cannot be connected to remote data from authored input.

## pvRenameArrays

Passes its input through unchanged except for array names. Each list property holds [current name, new name] pairs for one attribute type: points, cells, field data, graph vertices, graph edges or table rows. It accepts any data object, including composites and tables. Use it to give arrays the names a later step expects, e.g. to make datasets agree before pvAppendDatasets, or to replace solver names before export.

- Each list is flat: current name, then new name, repeated. Schemaxis rejects a list with an odd number of entries (INVALID_LENGTH) before the node runs.

## pvResampleAMR

Samples overlapping AMR data (vtkOverlappingAMR) onto a uniform grid covering the box from Min to Max with NumberofSamples points per axis, taking each value from the finest level that covers the sample. The result is a multiblock of uniform-grid partitions (NumberOfPartitions) with the fields on points (TransferToNodes true) or cells. Use it to compare AMR results with regular-grid data or to export a fixed-resolution image; use pvConvertAMRdatasettoMultiblock to keep the native blocks.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Min and Max both start at [0, 0, 0], which describes no region; always set the box.
- Parts of the box outside the AMR domain are trimmed, so the grid may have fewer points than requested.
- Input data are assumed cell-centred and rectilinear AMR is not supported.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvResampleToImage

Samples the input's point and cell arrays onto a new uniform image (vtkImageData) with SamplingDimensions points along x, y and z, spanning the input bounds (UseInputBounds, ParaView default) or custom SamplingBounds. Values are interpolated at the image points by a probe filter, so cell arrays also become point arrays, and points outside the input get 0 in the vtkValidPointMask array. Use it to convert unstructured results to a regular grid for image writers, volume rendering or pvHistogram2D; resample probes onto an existing mesh instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Memory grows with the product of the dimensions: the default 100 × 100 × 100 is a million points per array.
- Sampling is point-wise without averaging, so features smaller than the spacing can be missed.

## pvResampleToLine

Same native filter as pvPlotOverLine (vtkPVProbeLineFilter) with a different starting configuration: uniform sampling with Resolution 40 and the SamplingPattern hidden in ParaView's GUI. It returns a polyline with the input arrays interpolated along Point1-Point2 plus arc_length and vtkValidPointMask. Use it for a light uniform resampling, e.g. a coarse profile to compare between runs; use pvPlotOverLine or probeLine for detailed profiles.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Omitted, Point1 and Point2 are never the static [0, 0, 0]: in a bounded native probe with a polydata upstream a batch run read (1, 1, 1) and (-1, -1, -1), a line unrelated to the data (composite inputs give other uninitialised-bounds corners, by the source), and when the upstream already had data they were the corners of its bounding box. Always set both.
- Points outside the data are flagged by vtkValidPointMask 0; exclude them before computing statistics.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvResourceImageTexture

Typed texture resource (vtkTexture) that loads its image from a file such as a PNG or JPEG. It produces no dataset: other nodes reference it through texture inputs, currently pvLogo's Texture port, and several consumers may share it. Use it when the picture is a file on disk; use pvResourceTexture when the image comes from a pipeline node.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- FileName is required and is read by ParaView's image reader; unsupported image formats fail at update.
- Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-textures.json (receipt in verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

Inputs: none.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ColorMode` | When color mode is Default, 8-bits textures is equivalent to Direct Scalars, while equivalent to Map Scalars for 16-bits textures. In the case of Map Scalars, all the values are mapped to a generic color map. | `{"type":"enum","values":["Default","Map Scalars","Direct Scalars"]}` | omitted |
| `FileName` | Set the name of image file to load. | `{"minLength":1,"type":"string"}` | **required** |

| `RestrictPowerOf2ImageSmaller` | Rendering-only choice used when an image exceeds the graphics card's maximum texture size and must be resampled to power-of-two dimensions: true rounds each dimension down (smaller, blurrier texture), false rounds up. It never changes the image data that consumers such as pvLogo receive. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

## pvResourcePVLookupTable

Typed colour lookup-table resource (vtkPVDiscretizableColorTransferFunction) that maps data values to colours, either as a continuous colour map defined by RGBPoints control points or as categorical colours for annotated values (InterpretValuesAsCategories). It is not a dataset: it is connected to lookup-table inputs such as pvColorByArray, pvOMETIFFChannelCalculator or the PLY and OpenVDB writers, and several consumers can share one table. Scene appearances build their own colour maps from field, range and preset, so use this resource only for those explicit ports.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- RGBPoints positions are data values; ParaView's GUI usually rescales a new map to the data range, but here nothing rescales it, so set positions that cover your array's range.
- Optional ScalarOpacityFunction and TransferFunction2D inputs accept pvResourcePiecewiseFunction and pvResourceTransferFunction2D nodes.
- Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json and paraview-writer-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

## pvResourcePiecewiseFunction

Typed piecewise-function resource (vtkPiecewiseFunction) that maps a data value to a single number, normally opacity from 0 to 1, through control points. Its main use is the ScalarOpacityFunction input of pvResourcePVLookupTable, where it defines how transparent each data value is. It produces no dataset and can be shared by several lookup tables.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Points positions are data values and are not rescaled automatically; place them across your array's range.
- Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); other settings are unverified.

Native binding: `PiecewiseFunction`. Output kind: `["piecewise-function"]`.

Coverage: `{"defaults":"native defaults for omitted options","gaps":{},"origin":"generated","output":"process-local typed native resource","outputPorts":null,"qualification":"not-run"}`.

Inputs: none.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AllowDuplicateScalars` | Whether two control points may share the same x value. True keeps both, giving a vertical step in opacity at that value; false makes the later point replace the earlier one. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `Points` | Control points as a flat list of [x, y, midpoint, sharpness] groups: x is the data value, y the function value there (usually opacity 0 to 1), midpoint (0 to 1) where between this point and the next the value is halfway, and sharpness from 0 (linear) to 1 (step). Give groups in increasing x. | `{"items":{"type":"number"},"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `ScalarRangeInitialized` | Set to 1 to indicate that the scalar range has been initialized. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `UseLogScale` | When true, the position between two control points is measured on a log10 scale of the data value, so the function changes evenly per decade rather than per unit. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

- `Points` requires complete groups of 4 values.

## pvResourceTransferFunction2D

Typed two-dimensional transfer-function resource (vtkPVTransferFunction2D): colour and opacity defined over two axes, usually a scalar on x and a second quantity such as gradient magnitude on y, as used by ParaView's 2-D volume rendering. It is built from coloured rectangles (Boxes) within Range and sampled to an image of OutputDimensions. In Schemaxis it only connects to the TransferFunction2D input of pvResourcePVLookupTable; Schemaxis scene appearances do not perform volume rendering.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Creating it has no visible effect in Schemaxis images; it is relevant only if a consumer uses the lookup table's 2-D function.
- Exercised by examples/schemaxis/paraview-resources.json (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); its rendering effect is unverified.

## pvRestartedSimExodusReader

Reads an Exodus simulation that was restarted, through a metadata file listing the output file sets of each restart, so they behave as one continuous time series. The output and the block, set, map and variable selections are those of pvExodusIIReader: a multiblock of unstructured grids with nodal and element variables, displacements applied by default. Use pvExodusIIReader for a single run's files.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- FileName must name the restart metadata file, not one of the Exodus files.
- FilePattern, FilePrefix and XMLFileName are optional, as their ParaView file lists are marked optional. Leave them out to read FileName as given: FilePattern and FilePrefix rebuild the file name from a printf-style pattern, so supplying them changes which file is read, and XMLFileName names an optional part and material description.
- VTK's Exodus reader starts with every result variable disabled; list the PointVariables and ElementVariables you need, or the blocks arrive without fields.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvRestartedSimSpyPlotReader

Reads a CTH (Spy Plot) simulation that was restarted, through a metadata file (.spcth-timeseries) listing the output file sets of each restart, so the sets behave as one continuous time series. Output port 0 is the volume data (hierarchical blocks with cell-centred arrays such as material volume fractions), port 1 the tracers and port 2 the markers; select a port with {"node": id, "port": n}. Use pvSpyPlotReader for a single .spcth case and pvspcthhistoryreader for history files.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- FileName must name the restart metadata file, not one of the individual .spcth case files.
- Fields are cell-centred; convert with cellToPoint before operations that need point data.

## pvReverseSense

Flips the orientation of polygonal data: ReverseCells (ParaView default true) reverses each cell's point order, which flips its implied front face, and ReverseNormals (default false) multiplies existing point and cell normals by −1. Use it when a surface's normals point inward, e.g. an STL with clockwise winding, before shading, normal-based glyphs or operations that assume outward orientation; normals with consistency orients a surface automatically.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Reversing cells while an existing Normals array is left unchanged makes them disagree; enable ReverseNormals too when normals are present.
- ReverseNormals has no effect if the input carries no normals.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvRibbon

Turns lines and polylines (polydata, e.g. streamlines) into flat ribbon strips that follow each line. The ribbon's orientation comes from a normal: the 3-component point array chosen in Vectors, or the fixed DefaultNormal when UseDefaultNormal is true; with neither, VTK computes sliding normals for each line. Width is the half-width; VaryWidth scales it along the line by the Scalars array from Width at the array minimum to twice Width at its maximum, and Angle rotates the ribbon about the line. Use tube or pvTube for round tubes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The Vectors array sets the ribbon normal, not the flow direction; selecting the velocity itself, which is tangent to a streamline, gives degenerate ribbons.
- Lines with duplicate consecutive points, or normals parallel to the line, are skipped; run clean first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `Ribbon`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvRotationalExtrusion

Sweeps polygonal data around an axis through the coordinate origin (RotationAxis, ParaView default z) to build a swept surface: free edges and lines become surfaces and vertices become lines, so a profile curve becomes an axisymmetric shell (cylinder, bottle), and Translation or DeltaRadius turn it into a spring or spiral. Capping closes the ends with copies of a filled 2-D input. Output is polydata, a surface rather than a volume; use pvVolumeOfRevolution to sweep 2-D cells into volume cells.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The axis passes through (0, 0, 0); translate the profile first (transform) if the physical axis is elsewhere.
- Closed surfaces such as a sphere have no free edges, so they give no swept surface, only caps.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `RotationalExtrusion`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

This works property if the input is a 2D surface composed of filled polygons. If the input dataset is a closed solid (e.g., a sphere), then either two copies of the dataset will be drawn or no surface will be drawn. No surface is drawn if either this property is set to 0 or if the two surfaces would occupy exactly the same 3D space (i.e., the Angle property's value is a multiple of 360, and the values of the Translation and DeltaRadius properties are 0). | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

## pvSAVGReader

Reads a NIST SAVG file (.savg), a plain-text format of coloured points, lines and polygons used for immersive-visualization scenes. The output is a partitioned dataset collection with one polydata partition per primitive kind found (points, lines, polygons), with optional "rgba_colors" and "vertex_normals" point arrays. Use it to bring such scene geometry into a pipeline; it carries no simulation fields.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The file name must end in .savg; the reader ignores any other name and produces nothing.
- Primitives such as tri, pixel, text and program lines are skipped as unsupported.

## pvSEPReader

Reads Stanford Exploration Project seismic data: a text .H header describing up to 32 named axes (labels such as CDP, LINE, OFFSET, DEPTH) with their sizes, origins and sampling, which points to the raw .H@ data file. You choose which named axes become the output x, y and z (or x and y for 2-D output) and hold the remaining axes at one index each; the result is uniform image data with an ImageScalars array.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Axis names must match the header labels; when the header has no labels, VTK assigns the default names to the first axes in order.
- Choose different axes for x, y, z and the fixed dimensions; reusing one axis collapses that direction.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSLACDataReader

Reads the NetCDF-based mesh and mode files of SLAC's accelerator electromagnetics codes (Omega3P, Tau3P and related tools). MeshFileName is the element mesh; ModeFileName is one mode file (usually an eigenmode with electric and magnetic fields) or several files forming a time series. Output port 0 (External Surface) is the boundary surface and port 1 (Entire Volume) the volume mesh, filled only when ReadInternalVolume is enabled. When a mode file stores a frequency (100 or more, treated as hertz) the complex fields are animated over one period of the lowest frequency: each mode contributes magnitude × FrequencyScale × cos(initial phase + 2πft + PhaseShift) and the modes are summed.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Port 0 is only the external surface; enable ReadInternalVolume and connect {"node": id, "port": 1} for fields inside the cavity.
- ModeFileName is optional: omit it to read the mesh alone. A bounded native probe on 2026-10-12 (ParaView 5.13.3, serial, synthetic one-tetrahedron mesh) read the mesh with ModeFileName omitted, with no error (4 points, 4 cells); it has not been run on real SLAC files.
- Mode files must use the same points as the mesh file.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

Native binding: `SLACDataReader`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvSPHDatasetInterpolator

Interpolates particle data with smoothed-particle-hydrodynamics kernels: the Input is the particle set (a point set with point arrays, normally including density and optionally mass) and the Source is any dataset whose points receive the SPH-weighted values. The output keeps Source's structure and adds the interpolated arrays, a Shepard-sum array (on by default) and any derivative arrays. Use it to post-process SPH simulation output on meshes, slices or images; for non-SPH scattered data use pvPointDatasetInterpolator.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The kernel SpatialStep (smoothing length h) defaults to 0.0001; set it to the simulation's smoothing length in dataset units, or neighbourhoods are tiny and most output points become null points.
- DensityArray defaults to the name Rho; name your particle density array if it differs.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSPHLineInterpolator

Interpolates SPH particle data (Input) with SPH kernels onto a high-resolution straight line set in the Source options (Point1, Point2, Resolution; ParaView default 1000 intervals), producing a polyline profile with the interpolated arrays and a Shepard-sum array, e.g. a density or pressure profile through a particle simulation.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The line endpoints may be derived by ParaView from the input bounds, but Schemaxis has not verified that; their static default is [0, 0, 0] for both, a degenerate line. Set Point1 and Point2 explicitly in dataset coordinates.

## pvSTEPReader

Reads a STEP CAD file through OpenCASCADE and tessellates its B-rep faces into triangles, giving a multiblock dataset with one polydata block per shape (named from the file, or Unnamed) and a per-cell Colors array from the CAD colours. LinearDeflection and AngularDeflection set how closely the triangles follow curved surfaces; ReadWire adds edges as polylines. Use it to bring CAD geometry in for rendering, clipping or probing; use pvIGESReader for .iges, and readSTL or pvSTLReader for already-tessellated STL.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- VTK applies no unit conversion; compare the output bounds with the simulation's length unit before combining them.
- LinearDeflection is an absolute distance in model units unless RelativeDeflection is on; the default 0.1 can be very coarse for small parts, so scale it to the model size.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so check the output on your own files.

Native binding: `STEPReader`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

Coverage: `{"defaults":"native defaults for omitted options","gaps":{},"origin":"generated","output":"native inspection required; explicit output-port selection available","outputPorts":null,"qualification":"not-run"}`.

Inputs: none.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AngularDeflection` | Limits the angle between two subsequent segments. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `FileNames` | The list of files to be read by the reader. If more than one file is specified, the reader will switch to file series mode in which it will pretend that it can support time and provide one file per time step. | `{"items":{"minLength":1,"type":"string"},"minItems":1,"type":"array"}` | **required** |
| `LinearDeflection` | Limits the distance between a curve and the resulting tesselation. | `{"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `ReadWire` | Determines if 1D cells will be read. If enabled, surface boundaries are read. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `RelativeDeflection` | Determines if the deflection values are relative to object size. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

- `FileNames` is a constructor option.

## pvSTLReader

Full native STL reader: reads ASCII or binary stereolithography files (.stl) into triangle polydata, and a list of several files into a time series. In ParaView 5.13.3 this proxy exposes only the file list (the ScalarTags option of the core reader is not exposed). For a single CAD surface the curated readSTL does the same with one file.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- STL carries no units; check millimetres versus metres before combining with simulation data.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvScatterPlot

ParaView's Scatter Plot: passes a dataset through unchanged (vtkPassThrough) and marks it for the plot-matrix view, which shows every pair of arrays as a scatter plot in the ParaView GUI. In Schemaxis the data result is the unchanged input.

- No plot or table is computed; to get values for plotting, convert to a table, e.g. with pvExtractAttributes.

## pvSegYReader

Reads a SEG-Y seismic file. 3-D surveys become a structured grid (default) or, with StructuredGrid false, a lighter image data whose positions and shape may be approximate; 2-D lines become a structured grid sheet. Axes are crossline, inline and depth, and the trace samples are the point values. Trace positions come from source, CDP or custom header bytes, and VerticalCRS decides whether the vertical axis is height (positive up) or depth.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The extended textual header is not read, so check VerticalCRS against the survey documentation.
- In Custom XYCoordMode set both XCoordByte and YCoordByte: ParaView's initial YCoordByte is 76, not the SEG-Y source-Y byte 77.
- Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

Use it for 2-D lines whose headers would otherwise be misread as 3-D. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `StructuredGrid` | Specify if we create a Structured Grid even when the data is SEG-Y 3D. If we set this option to false we create an Image Data for a SEG-Y 3D dataset. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

## pvSelectionQuerySource

Creates a query selection, ParaView's "Find Data" mechanism: QueryString is a structured query over the input's arrays, element indices or locations, evaluated per element when pvExtractSelection (or another extractor) runs; the elements where it is true are selected. ElementType chooses cells (ParaView default) or points, and Selectors can restrict the query to some blocks of a composite input. The output is a vtkSelection (no geometry) for the Selection port of pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. For a plain range on one array, pvThresholdSelectionSource is simpler.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView evaluates query text as Python (vtkPythonSelector, paraview.detail.calculator), so Schemaxis accepts only the structured QueryString, generates the text itself and checks it again before assignment; the selection still needs a ParaView build with Python and numpy.
- Leave ContentType at 9 (QUERY) and FieldTypeOption at 1; the other values make this source produce a different, empty selection type.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvShrink

Moves the points of every cell toward that cell's centroid (average of its points) by ShrinkFactor, separating cells so individual elements become visible; output is an unstructured grid with unshared points. It is a mesh-inspection aid, not a geometric operation for measurements; the curated shrink offers the same with a Schemaxis default.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Shrunk cells no longer share points, so connectivity-based operations see disjoint cells.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSlice

ParaView's general Slice filter: cuts any dataset (or hyper tree grid) with an implicit surface (Plane, Box, Sphere or Cylinder) and returns polygonal data, i.e. surfaces from volumes and lines from surfaces, with point data interpolated. SliceOffsetValues produces several parallel copies of the cut surface in one node, and Crinkle slice instead keeps the whole input cells crossed by the surface. Use slice for a simple plane with Schemaxis defaults, pvSliceWithPlane for a faster multithreaded plane cut, or pvAxisAlignedSlice for hyper tree grids.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Unless set, the plane origin and normal are ParaView's initial values, which may depend on the input bounds; set SliceType options explicitly for reproducible cuts.
- For Sphere, Cylinder and Box slice types an offset is a value of the implicit function, not a distance; see SliceOffsetValues.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSliceAlongPolyLine

Cuts a dataset with the curtain surface swept by moving a polyline parallel to the z-axis, like a vertical cross-section along a ship track, river or flight path. Connect the dataset to Dataset and the path (polydata containing a polyline) to PolyLine; the result is polygonal data with interpolated attributes. Only the polyline's x-y path matters. For a single straight cut use pvSlice or slice.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The sweep direction is always the z-axis; rotate the data first (transform) if the vertical direction of your model is another axis.
- If parts of the curtain are missing, increase Tolerance.

## pvSliceWithPlane

Fast, multithreaded plane cut (vtkPVPlaneCutter) of any dataset, composite dataset, overlapping AMR or hyper tree grid, producing polygonal data with interpolated point data and transferred cell data. It accepts only planes (Plane or Axis Aligned Plane) and, for unstructured input, can build a sphere tree to accelerate repeated cuts. Choose it over pvSlice when a plane is all you need and speed matters, or when slicing AMR data at a chosen level; use pvSlice for spheres, boxes, cylinders or offset copies.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Duplicated points along cell edges are not merged by default; enable Mergeduplicatedpointsintheslice before operations that need a connected surface, such as connectivity or feature edges.
- Set the Plane options explicitly; ParaView's initial origin may depend on the input bounds.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSmooth

Laplacian smoothing of a polygonal surface: each point moves iteratively toward the average of its connected neighbours, for up to NumberofIterations (ParaView default 20) or until the largest motion falls below Convergence. VTK's relaxation factor of 0.01 keeps each step small. Connectivity, point count and arrays are unchanged. Use it to reduce noise or faceting of scanned or iso-surfaces; smooth is the curated version.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Laplacian smoothing shrinks the surface and rounds edges; use few iterations when dimensions matter.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSpatioTemporalHarmonics

Adds a point array SpatioTemporalHarmonics (set as active scalars) whose value at point x and time t is the sum over harmonics of A·sin(k·x + ω·t + φ), with t the requested pipeline time and x in dataset coordinates. It produces analytic, time-varying test fields, e.g. to check interpolation, temporal statistics or FFT workflows against known waves.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The ParaView default harmonics are examples sized for bounds [-10, 10] and times in [0, 2π); give your own for other domains.
- There is no 2π factor: ω and k are angular (radians per time unit and per length unit).
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSpatioTemporalHarmonicsUniformGrid

Generates image data (a uniform grid with spacing 1 over WholeExtent) with a time-dependent point array "SpatioTemporalHarmonics" = Σ A·sin(ω·t + k·x + φ), summed over the listed harmonics, at each listed time step. ## pvSphere

Creates a polygonal sphere (or a section of one) with point normals: radius Radius around Center, tessellated by ThetaResolution longitude and PhiResolution latitude divisions. StartTheta/EndTheta (around z, 0 to 360 degrees) and StartPhi/EndPhi (from +z at 0 to -z at 180 degrees) cut out partial spheres. Use it as reference geometry or a probe surface; the curated sphere operation offers Schemaxis defaults.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default resolution (8 × 8) is coarse; raise both resolutions for smooth rendering or accurate probing.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvSpyPlotReader

Reads a CTH Spy Plot case: an ASCII .spcth case file listing the binary files that hold the data. Output port 0 is the volume data (a hierarchical composite of blocks with cell-centred arrays), port 1 the tracers and port 2 the markers. By ParaView default it derives material densities from selected material mass and volume fraction and merges X/Y/Z component arrays into vectors. Use pvRestartedSimSpyPlotReader for a restarted run split over several file sets and pvspcthhistoryreader for history files.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Fields are cell-centred block data; convert with cellToPoint before operations that need point data, such as streamline tracing.
- Derived densities need both Material Mass and Material Volume Fraction arrays selected.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvStreakLine

Computes streaklines in an unsteady (time-dependent) vector field: particles are released from every SeedSource point at each input time step and advected through the changing field, and the particles released from the same place are joined into lines, the analogue of continuous dye injection. ParaView requests the input time steps itself, from the first step up to the requested time, so the input must have at least two time steps and a 3-component point vector field. Output is polydata (polylines, single points as vertices) with ParticleAge, ParticleId, InjectedPointId and the interpolated input arrays. Use pvStreamTracer for a steady snapshot and pvTemporalParticlesToPathlines to draw trails of existing particles.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- In the VTK used by ParaView 5.13.3 the streakline filter forces reinjection at every step, so ForceReinjectionEveryNSteps has no effect here; StaticSeeds and DisableResetCache are also no-ops.
- Every requested time integrates from the first time step, which is slow on long series; restrict the input time range first.
- Velocity must be point data; convert cell-centred solver output with cellToPoint.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `StreakLine`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvStreamTracer

Integrates steady streamlines through one time step of a 3-component vector field, forward, backward or both, from seeds made by the built-in SeedType generator (Point Cloud, the ParaView default, or Line). The output is polydata polylines carrying the input point arrays interpolated along each line, IntegrationTime, and cell arrays SeedIds and ReasonForTermination (1 left the domain, 4 maximum length, 5 maximum steps, 6 below terminal speed); with ComputeVorticity on (ParaView default) Vorticity, Rotation, AngularVelocity and Normals are added. Use the curated streamTracer for the common case, pvStreamTracerWithCustomSource to seed from another node's points, and pvStreakLine or pvTemporalParticlesToPathlines for unsteady flow.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Step lengths default to Cell Length units (fractions of a cell), not dataset lengths; set IntegrationStepUnit to Length before giving steps in metres.
- MaximumStreamlineLength has a static default of 1.0 that ParaView may replace with the input size; set it explicitly, or long streamlines can be cut short in large domains.
- Cell-centred velocity is accepted, but vorticity is then 0; convert with cellToPoint first when vorticity or smooth interpolation matters.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvStreamTracerWithCustomSource

Integrates steady streamlines like pvStreamTracer, but every point of a second input (SeedSource) that lies inside the dataset starts a streamline, so any node's points can seed it: a probe line, a slice, an inlet patch or points read from a file. The vector field must be point-centred with 3 components. The output is polydata polylines carrying the input point arrays interpolated along each line, IntegrationTime, and cell arrays SeedIds and ReasonForTermination (1 left the domain, 4 maximum length, 5 maximum steps, 6 below terminal speed); with ComputeVorticity on (ParaView default) Vorticity, Rotation, AngularVelocity and Normals are added. With direction BOTH, N seeds give up to 2N lines.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Step lengths default to Cell Length units (fractions of a cell), not dataset lengths; set IntegrationStepUnit to Length before giving steps in metres.
- MaximumStreamlineLength has a static default of 1.0 that ParaView may replace with the input size; set it explicitly, or long streamlines can be cut short in large domains.
- A seed source with thousands of points produces thousands of lines; use a coarser seed node.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSubdivide

Refines a triangle mesh linearly: each pass splits every triangle into four by adding a point at the midpoint of each edge, so the original surface shape and points are kept exactly while the resolution increases. Use it to give a coarse triangulated surface more points before interpolating onto it, warping or sampling. Input must be polydata of triangles (run triangulate first); use pvLoopSubdivision for a smoothed surface.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each pass quadruples the triangle count; four passes give 256 times as many triangles.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSuperquadric

Creates a superquadric surface with normals and texture coordinates: one family covering ellipsoids, rounded boxes, cylinders and tori, chosen by the ThetaRoundness and PhiRoundness exponents (1 = round, near 0 = square-edged, above 1 = pinched). With Toroidal true (the ParaView default) it is a torus-like ring whose hole size is set by Thickness. Use it for test geometry or glyph shapes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView's default is a torus (Toroidal true), unlike VTK's own default; set Toroidal false for an ellipsoid-like solid.
- Size and Thickness are shape coefficients, so the overall extent is not exactly Size.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvSurfaceFlow

Computes the net flux of a point vector field through a surface: at each point it takes the dot product of the vector with a normal averaged from the neighbouring 2-D cells, then integrates it over the surface with Integrate Variables. The output is a one-point unstructured grid whose point array Surface Flow holds the integral (vector units times area), e.g. a volumetric flow rate when the vector is velocity. Use it on a slice, a boundary patch or any 2-D surface; integrate gives other surface integrals.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only 2-D cells (triangles, quads, polygons, pixels) contribute; feed a surface, not a volume mesh.
- Point normals are made mutually consistent but their overall sign follows the first cell's orientation, so the flux sign may be reversed; check it against a known inflow.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSurfaceNormals

Computes point normals (array Normals) on polygonal surfaces by averaging the normals of the polygons around each point, for smooth shading and for operations that need surface normals. By ParaView default polygon ordering is made consistent and points are split along edges sharper than FeatureAngle (30 degrees), keeping edges crisp but duplicating points; cell normals can be output too. The curated normals operation uses the same algorithm with Schemaxis defaults (splitting off).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Splitting (default true) duplicates points along sharp edges, changing point count and connectivity; turn it off before operations that need the original points.
- Normals follow polygon ordering; on open or inconsistently ordered surfaces some may point inward, so check orientation or use FlipNormals.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `SurfaceNormals`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `Consistency` | The value of this property controls whether consistent polygon ordering is enforced. Generally the normals for a data set should either all point inward or all point outward. If the value of this property is 1, then this filter will reorder the points of cells that whose normal vectors are oriented the opposite direction from the rest of those in the data set. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `FeatureAngle` | The value of this property defines a feature edge. If the surface normal between two adjacent triangles is at least as large as this Feature Angle, a feature edge exists. If Splitting is on, points are duplicated along these feature edges. (See the Splitting property.) | `{"maximum":180.0,"minimum":0.0,"type":"number"}` | omitted |
| `FlipNormals` | If the value of this property is 1, this filter will reverse the normal direction (and reorder the points accordingly) for all polygons in the data set; this changes front-facing polygons to back-facing ones, and vice versa. You might want to do this if your viewing position will be inside the data set instead of outside of it. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `NonManifoldTraversal` | Turn on/off traversal across non-manifold edges. Not traversing non-manifold edges will prevent problems where the consistency of polygonal ordering is corrupted due to topological loops. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

| `Splitting` | This property controls the splitting of sharp edges. If sharp edges are split (property value = 1), then points are duplicated along these edges, and separate normals are computed for both sets of points to give crisp (rendered) surface definition. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |


## pvSurfaceTangents

Computes per-point tangent vectors (array Tangents) of a triangulated surface from its point normals and texture coordinates, as required for normal-map texturing in rendering. The input must be triangle polydata with point Normals and texture coordinates; the output is the same polydata with tangents added. Use it only for textured rendering; it has no analysis meaning.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Missing normals or texture coordinates make the filter fail; run normals and a texture-mapping step (e.g. pvTextureMaptoPlane) first, and triangulate general polygons.

## pvSurfaceVectors

Constrains a point vector field on a 2-D surface relative to the local surface normal (averaged from neighbouring 2-D cells). Parallel removes the normal component, leaving the tangential part (e.g. wall shear direction or surface streamlines); Perpendicular keeps only the normal component; PerpendicularScale outputs the signed normal component as a new scalar array named Perpendicular Scale. The modified vectors keep the input array name; geometry is unchanged. pvSurfaceFlow uses the PerpendicularScale mode internally to compute fluxes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Works on point vectors and 2-D cells only; volume cells are ignored when computing normals.
- The normal sign follows the cell orientation, so PerpendicularScale values may have the opposite sign to the outward normal.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvSynchronizeTime

Snaps the time values of one dataset to those of another. DataToPass supplies the data and its time steps; any of its time values within RelativeTolerance × (its time range) of a TimeToSync time value is replaced by that value, so both sources report identical times, e.g. a simulation written at 0.1000001 s and experimental data at 0.1 s. The output keeps DataToPass's data and number of time steps; only the time labels change.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Data are not interpolated in time; for different sampling use a temporal interpolator.
- Two input steps that snap to the same value become ambiguous; ParaView warns about this.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.
