## pvTableFFT

Computes the discrete Fourier transform of every numeric column of a table (columns whose names start with vtk are skipped; 2-component columns are treated as complex), returning a table of spectra. The sampling rate is taken from a column named Time (any capitalization, assumed evenly spaced) or else from DefaultSampleRate (ParaView default 10000 Hz), and a Frequency column is added by default. Use it for spectra of probe histories, e.g. pressure fluctuations over time from a plot-over-time table; enable UseWelchMethod for an averaged, smoother spectrum of long noisy signals.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Unevenly spaced time samples give wrong frequencies; resample the history to a constant step first.
- Without a Time column the 10000 Hz default rate is used, which is almost never the true rate; add the time column or set DefaultSampleRate.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `TableFFT`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvTableToStructuredGrid

Turns a table into a curvilinear structured grid: X, Y and Z columns give the point coordinates, row order is point order with i varying fastest, then j, then k, and the other columns become point arrays. WholeExtent gives the grid's index ranges, and the table must have exactly (imax-imin+1)(jmax-jmin+1)(kmax-kmin+1) rows. Use it for gridded data exported row by row, e.g. a CSV of a structured solver block; use pvTableToPoints for scattered points.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- With the ParaView default WholeExtent [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] only a one-row table fits; always set the extent to match the table.
- Rows must be ordered i fastest; a table sorted differently gives a scrambled grid.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTemporalArrayOperator

Combines one array at two of the input's stored time steps, chosen by zero-based indices (FirstTimeStepIndex, SecondTimeStepIndex), with +, -, * or / applied value by value as first-operator-second. The output is the dataset at the second step plus one new array named after the input array with a suffix (by default _add, _sub, _mul or _div), e.g. p_sub for the pressure change between two saved times. Both steps must hold the array with the same number of tuples and components, so the mesh must not change. Use temporalStatistics or pvTemporalStatistics for averages over all steps.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Both indices default to 0, which combines the first step with itself (ParaView only warns); set both.
- The input must report at least two time steps; indices count stored steps from 0, they are not time values.
- For integer arrays / is integer division; convert to floating point first (calculator).
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTemporalCache

Keeps copies of the input at up to CacheSize recently requested time steps (ParaView default 2, range 2 to 10) and returns a cached copy when the same time is requested again, instead of re-running the upstream pipeline. Data and time values are unchanged. It helps when downstream temporal filters, e.g. pvTemporalInterpolator, repeatedly request the same steps from an expensive reader or filter chain.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each cached step keeps a copy of the dataset in memory; keep CacheSize small for large meshes.

## pvTemporalCacheSource

The same cache as pvTemporalCache (vtkTemporalDataSetCache), registered by ParaView as a source with IsASource true, the configuration meant for Catalyst in-situ pipelines: it then reports only the times currently held in the cache as its time steps and keeps entries even when the upstream pipeline changes, so it can hold a short history of a live simulation. For post-processing stored results use pvTemporalCache.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Because entries are not invalidated when upstream settings change, results can be stale; use pvTemporalCache in ordinary pipelines.

## pvTemporalInterpolator

Linearly interpolates point coordinates and point and cell arrays between the two stored time steps around a requested time, so data can be obtained at times the input did not save; ParaView uses vtkAdaptiveTemporalInterpolator, which also copes when the mesh appears to change between steps. By ParaView default it reports the input's own steps; DiscreteTimeStepInterval reports evenly spaced steps instead and ResampleFactor adds steps inside each stored interval. The input needs at least two time steps, and interpolated values are a linear approximation, not solver results.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Schemaxis updates every node at the scene time, and the curated foam reader rejects times it has not stored (TIME_UNAVAILABLE), so intermediate scene times are refused at a foam node before this filter runs.
- Linear interpolation smooths over events between saved steps; save output more often when such detail matters.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTemporalParticlesToPathlines

Builds trails from moving particles: it takes a point set whose points move between time steps (e.g. Lagrangian particles read from a solver, or a particle tracer's output) and joins each particle's successive positions into a polyline. ParaView loops over the input times itself up to the requested time. Output port 0 (Pathlines) holds the trails with TrailId and TrackLength; port 1 (Particles) holds one vertex at each trail's head. Particles are matched by IdChannelArray (global ids or point index by default). Use pvStreakLine to compute particle motion from a velocity field instead.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- By ParaView default only every 100th point is tracked (MaskPoints) and trails keep 25 steps; set MaskPoints to 1 and raise MaxTrackLength for complete paths.
- If particles are reordered between steps, matching by index scrambles the trails; set IdChannelArray to a persistent particle id.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTemporalShiftScale

Relabels time without touching the data: an input time t is reported as (t + PreShift) × Scale + PostShift, and a request for output time T fetches input time (T − PostShift) / Scale − PreShift. Use it to align runs that started at different times, change time units (Scale 0.001 turns milliseconds into seconds), or repeat a cyclic dataset with Periodic. Nothing is resampled; use pvTemporalInterpolator for in-between states.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The upstream description gives the transform as t*Shift + Scale; the native code applies PreShift before scaling and PostShift after it, so the two shifts differ by a factor of Scale.
- Keep Scale non-zero; the backward conversion divides by it.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

If data exists for times {0,N-1}, setting periodic to true will cause time 0 to be produced when time N, 2N, 2N etc is requested. This effectively gives the source the ability to generate time data indefinitely in a loop. When combined with Shift/Scale, the time becomes periodic in the shifted and scaled time frame of reference. Note: Since the input time may not start at zero, the wrapping of time from the end of one period to the start of the next, will subtract the initial time - a source with T{5..6} repeated periodically will have output time {5..6..7..8} etc. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |

## pvTemporalSmoothing

Replaces each point and cell array value by its plain (unweighted) mean over a sliding window of 2 × TemporalWindowHalfWidth + 1 stored time steps centred on the requested step. The output is still temporal, but loses HalfWidth steps at each end of the series, and requests outside the remaining range use the nearest available step. Use it to suppress step-to-step noise in transient results; the number and order of points and cells must not change over time.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each output step updates the whole upstream pipeline once per window step, which can be expensive.
- Time spacing is ignored, so unevenly stored steps are weighted equally.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTemporalSnaptoTimeStep

Makes a request for any time return the data of one of the input's stored time steps: SnapMode picks the nearest stored step (ParaView default), the last step at or below, or the first step at or above the requested time. Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Nearest can serve a requested time from a later stored step; use NextBelowOrEqual when results must never come from the future.

## pvTemporalStatistics

Computes, for every point and cell array of a time-dependent input, its average, minimum, maximum and population standard deviation over all input time steps, which the filter requests itself. The output has the input's type and geometry, no time, and arrays named <name>_average, <name>_minimum, <name>_maximum and <name>_stddev (other arrays are not kept). Every step is weighted equally regardless of time spacing, so this is not a time integral. This is the generated binding with native names (ComputeAverage, …); the curated temporalStatistics does the same with shorter option names.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Unequal time steps bias the average; resample time first if the spacing varies.
- Every time step is read and processed, which can take long on large series; restrict the input time range first.
- The mesh must keep the same points and cells over time; on changing meshes the statistics are meaningless.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTensorGlyph

Places a glyph (sphere by ParaView default; cylinder, box or superquadric) at every point and scales and orients it by the eigen-decomposition of the symmetric part of a point tensor: the major eigenvalue scales the glyph's x axis along the major eigenvector, the medium y, the minor z. Tensors may have 9 components or 6 symmetric components ordered XX, YY, ZZ, XY, YZ, XZ. Output is polydata, by default coloured by input scalars. Use it for stress, strain or diffusion tensors; pvGlyph handles vectors.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Six-component tensors must use XX, YY, ZZ, XY, YZ, XZ; other orders (e.g. Voigt XX, YY, ZZ, YZ, XZ, XY) give wrong orientations.
- Glyph size is ScaleFactor times eigenvalue, so near singularities glyphs explode; enable LimitScalingByEigenvalues with a MaxScaleFactor.
- ParaView warns that glyphing every point of a structured grid can use much memory; subsample first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTensorPrincipalInvariants

Computes the principal values and principal directions of selected symmetric tensor arrays (for example stress or strain). For each selected array <name> it adds <name> - Sigma 1, 2 and 3 (values sorted from largest to smallest) and the matching <name> - Sigma n (Vector) direction arrays, keeping the input arrays. Accepted tensors have 6 components in the order XX, YY, ZZ, XY, YZ, XZ, or 3 components named XX, YY, XY for 2-D tensors. Use pvYieldCriteria when you need Tresca or von Mises values.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Full 9-component tensors are not accepted; extract the symmetric 6-component form first.
- A 3-component array is treated as a 2-D tensor only when its component names are exactly XX, YY and XY; otherwise it is ignored as a vector.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTessellate

Subdivides cells with non-linear geometry or fields (quadratic and higher-order cells) into linear simplices (tetrahedra, triangles or lines up to OutputDimension) until the chord error and optional per-field errors at edge midpoints fall below their limits, giving an unstructured grid that approximates curved geometry and fields with linear pieces. Use it before operations or exports that only handle linear cells; linear input is just split into simplices.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Output size grows quickly with MaximumNumberofSubdivisions, especially with OutputDimension 3.
- ChordError is in dataset length units; tighten it for small parts.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTextureMaptoCylinder

Adds 2-D texture coordinates (point array "Texture Coordinates") by projecting each point onto a cylinder: s follows the angle around the axis and t the position along it, 0 at Point1 and 1 at Point2. ## pvTextureMaptoPlane

Adds 2-D texture coordinates (point array "Texture Coordinates") by projecting each point onto a plane. In automatic mode (ParaView default, used while Origin and Point1 are both [0, 0, 0]) a least-squares plane is fitted and s and t run from 0 to 1 across the projected bounds. Otherwise s is the projection of (point − Origin) on Point1 − Origin, divided by that edge's squared length, and t likewise with Point2, so s and t are 0 at Origin and 1 at Point1 or Point2. Use it to drape an image (e.g. a photograph or map) on a flat or gently curved surface; pvTextureMaptoCylinder suits round parts.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- While Automatic is true the explicit points are used only if Origin or Point1 is non-zero, and Point2 alone is ignored; set Automatic to false whenever you give the points.
- Automatic mode needs at least three points; smaller inputs get no texture coordinates.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvThreshold

Extracts the cells whose values of a chosen point or cell array satisfy a criterion (Between LowerThreshold and UpperThreshold, below the lower or above the upper), producing an unstructured grid (or a masked hyper tree grid). It exposes the full native control: component handling for vector arrays (one component, magnitude, All or Any), Invert, AllScalars for point data and a continuous cell range. Use threshold for the common inclusive range test with validated field names; use pvClip with a scalar clip for smooth cuts through cells.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Cells are kept or dropped whole; the boundary is staircase-shaped, not interpolated.
- With a point array and AllScalars true (ParaView default), a cell is kept only if all its points pass; set AllScalars false to keep cells touching the range.
- LowerThreshold and UpperThreshold may be initialized from the array range by ParaView; set both explicitly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvTube

Wraps every line or polyline of polygonal input in a tube of NumberofSides faces (ParaView default 6) and Radius, producing polydata surfaces. VaryRadius can make the radius follow a point scalar or vector array, up to RadiusFactor times Radius. The cross-section is oriented by the input's point Normals array, by normals generated along each line, or by DefaultNormal when UseDefaultNormal is true. Use it to render streamlines, particle paths or wire models in 3-D; tube is the curated version.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Duplicate consecutive points, or normals parallel to the line, make VTK skip that line; run clean first.
- Radius is in dataset units and ParaView may initialize it from the input extent (1 %); set it explicitly.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `Tube`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvUnstructuredCellTypes

Generates an unstructured grid made of one chosen cell type (linear, quadratic, Lagrange or Bezier lines, triangles, quads, tetrahedra, hexahedra, wedges, pyramids, polyhedra…) by filling a BlocksDimensions grid of unit blocks starting at the origin; one block may hold several cells (e.g. six pyramids). Point arrays "DistanceToCenter" and "Polynomial" give known fields. Use it to test how filters, writers or renderers handle a specific cell type or element order.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Lagrange tetrahedral meshes are not always conformal at block boundaries, as the native documentation warns.
- 1-D types use only the first blocks dimension and 2-D types the first two.

## pvUnstructuredNetCDFPOPreader

Reads Parallel Ocean Program (POP) NetCDF output (.pop.nc, .pop.ncdf) and converts its logically structured grid into an unstructured grid on a sphere: horizontal positions come from a companion GRID.nc file in the same folder, and each layer's depth_t is subtracted from an Earth radius of 6371000 (metres), so deeper layers lie closer to the sphere's centre. Stride subsamples and VOI crops the structured index space before conversion. Use pvNetCDFPOPreader for the structured form.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The GRID.nc file must sit beside the data file; without it the lat-lon mapping fails.
- VerticalVelocity is computed only for a vector grid read over the full depth range with k stride 1.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

- Extents count files of the simulation decomposition, not grid cells or physical coordinates.

## pvValidateCells

Checks every cell for defects that break other filters and adds a cell array ValidityState: 0 for a valid cell, otherwise a bit field of problems such as wrong number of points, intersecting edges or faces, non-contiguous edges, non-convexity, or wrongly oriented faces. Geometry and arrays pass through. Use it to diagnose meshes that fail in clipping, integration or export, then threshold on ValidityState to locate bad cells.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Non-convex cells are flagged even though many meshes (e.g. polyhedral CFD meshes) use them legitimately; interpret flags per cell type.
- The geometric tolerance is VTK's default (not exposed in ParaView); very small cells can be misjudged.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvValueSelectionSource

Creates a value selection: elements whose value of ArrayName equals one of the listed integer values, e.g. all cells with MaterialId 3 or 7. The output is a vtkSelection (no geometry) for the Selection port of pvExtractSelection or pvAnnotateSelection. ParaView documents that it cannot select within composite datasets. Use pvThresholdSelectionSource for value ranges or floating-point data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The values are stored as vtkIdType integers and VTK's value selector only compares arrays of the same value type, so 32-bit integer or floating-point arrays may match nothing (VTK warns of a type mismatch); check the result, or use pvThresholdSelectionSource with narrow ranges.
- FieldType defaults to CELL; set POINT when the IDs or values refer to points, otherwise the wrong elements are matched.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvVisItAUXFileReader

Reads an ASCII .aux fluence file through VisIt's AUXFile plugin: the output is a 2-D rectilinear grid named "mesh" carrying one point array, "fluence". The format is documented only by the plugin source; choose this reader only for files written in that layout. FileName takes a list of files, each one time step of a series (ParaView's file-series wrapper).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

## pvVisItBOVReader

Reads VisIt's BOV (brick of values) format: a short text header (.bov) giving DATA_FILE, DATA_SIZE, DATA_FORMAT, BRICK_ORIGIN, BRICK_SIZE, VARIABLE and CENTERING for one raw binary array on a regular grid. The output is a rectilinear-grid block named "mesh" carrying that one variable. Use pvImageReader instead for raw volumes without a BOV header, where you supply dimensions, spacing and data type yourself. FileName takes a list of files, each one time step of a series (ParaView's file-series wrapper).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Whether the variable appears in PointArrayStatus or CellArrayStatus depends on the header's CENTERING (NODAL or ZONAL); select it in the matching list.
- Multi-component data arrive as one vector array; VisIt's real/imaginary expressions are not converted by the bridge.
- Name the arrays you need in PointArrayStatus and CellArrayStatus: the VisIt bridge starts with every variable unselected, so omitting them normally gives geometry without fields.

## pvVisItClawReader

Reads Clawpack/AMRClaw ASCII output through a small .claw boot file whose DIR=, TIME_FILES_SCANF/REGEX and GRID_FILES_SCANF/REGEX (and optional CYCLE_REGEX) lines locate the time-header and grid-data files. The output is a multiblock dataset in which "claw_mesh" holds every grid of every refinement level, with cell-centred solution components. The captured ParaView summary ("a material-ordered format very similar to IOUT=1") does not describe what the plugin source reads. One file supplies every time step the format stores.

- Write the .claw boot file yourself; pointing FileName at a fort.* data file does not work.

## pvVisItExtrudedVolReader

Reads VisIt's ExtrudedVol format: a text header (.exvol) naming a file stem, a chunk count, a time count and variables, with connectivity and variable files per chunk. Reads LAMMPS molecular-dynamics dump files (.dump, text with ITEM: sections) in which one file holds many time steps: each step becomes a time of a point mesh of atoms with the dumped per-atom columns as point arrays. ## pvVisItNASTRANReader

Reads NASTRAN bulk data decks (.nas) into one unstructured mesh named "mesh" with element groups as materials; no results are read. The native pvBDFReader reads NASTRAN bulk data in free format; this reader also handles fixed and large-field cards, so use it when the native reader rejects a deck. ## pvVisItNek5000Reader

Reads Nek5000 spectral-element CFD output through its small metadata file (.nek3d, .nek5000, …) whose filetemplate, firsttimestep and numtimesteps lines locate the field dumps. The output is the element mesh with node-centred velocity, pressure, temperature and scalars over time. The native pvNek5000Reader reads the same metadata file into an unstructured grid and is distributed; prefer it for parallel runs. One file supplies every time step the format stores.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The first dump in the series must contain the mesh coordinates; otherwise the read fails.
- Name the arrays you need in PointArrays and CellArrays: the VisIt bridge starts with every variable unselected, so omitting them normally gives geometry without fields.
- The VisIt plugin's own read options stay at their defaults; the ParaView proxy exposes no property to change them.

## pvVolumeOfRevolution

Sweeps a 2-D (planar) dataset about an axis to create a 3-D unstructured grid: vertices become lines, lines become quadrilaterals and 2-D cells become volume cells, with point and cell data copied to each swept copy. Use it to build a 3-D volume from an axisymmetric simulation for visualization or export. The axis is given by AxisPosition and AxisDirection (ParaView default: the x axis through the origin) and the sweep by SweepAngle and Resolution. ParaView's own short description of this filter (elevation) is a copying error.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The axis must not cross the geometry, or the output has intersecting cells.
- Vector arrays such as velocity are copied unchanged to every swept copy, not rotated; their components are only meaningful in the original plane.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvVoronoiMergeConnected

Merges the cells of a Voronoi tessellation that share the same global RegionId into single polyhedron cells (vtkPMergeConnected), turning per-particle Voronoi cells into one cell per connected region. ## pvVortexCores

Extracts vortex core lines with the parallel-vectors method: lines where velocity is parallel to acceleration (or to jerk with UseHigherOrderMethod). Candidate cells are prefiltered with the Q and delta criteria, and the output polylines carry q-criterion, delta-criterion, lambda_2-criterion, lambda_ci-criterion and vorticity_magnitude point arrays for further filtering. Only 3-D linear cells are processed and the vector field must be a 3-component point array. Use it to locate swirling-flow axes; for vortex regions rather than lines, compute Q or lambda2 with gradient and contour them.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Surface or 2-D meshes and higher-order cells produce no output; supply a linear volume mesh.
- The method is sensitive to noise and finds short spurious segments; threshold the output on the criterion arrays.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvWarpByScalar

Displaces each point along a direction by ScaleFactor × its scalar value: x' = x + ScaleFactor · s · n, with n the point normal when the input has normals and UseNormal is false, otherwise the constant Normal. XYPlane uses each point's z coordinate as s and warps along z (carpet plots). Polydata, structured and unstructured grids keep their type; image and rectilinear inputs become structured grids. Use it for elevation or carpet plots of a scalar on a surface; the curated warpScalar covers the common case.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- If the surface has point normals they are used unless UseNormal is true, so Normal may appear to be ignored.
- ScaleFactor stays 1.0 unless set (ParaView's NoDefault hint), so a scalar in pascals moves points by thousands of length units; choose a factor relative to the data range.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvWarpByVector

Displaces each point by ScaleFactor × a 3-component point vector (x' = x + ScaleFactor · v), e.g. structural displacements or mode shapes, to show the deformed shape. Point and cell data pass through, but input normals are dropped because the geometry changed. The curated warpVector covers the common case.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Use a ScaleFactor of 1 for true displacements; larger factors exaggerate deformation, so state the factor in published images.
- Recompute normals after warping for correct shading.

## pvWavelet

Generates image data over WholeExtent (spacing SubsampleRate, origin 0) with the point scalar "RTData" = Maximum·exp(-r²/(2·StandardDeviation²)) + XMag·sin(XFreq·x) + YMag·sin(YFreq·y) + ZMag·cos(ZFreq·z), where x, y, z are offsets from Center divided by the extent width on each axis and r is their length. It is ParaView's standard synthetic volume, used to test contouring, slicing, volume rendering and exports. The curated wavelet operation offers Schemaxis defaults.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The native documentation writes the terms as a product; VTK adds them, so the Gaussian and the waves superpose.
- Center is in index coordinates, not physical units, because spacing is 1 (or SubsampleRate).
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

It is not in physical units. ParaView's own text refers to "the equation" it prints, which multiplies the terms; the filter adds them to the Gaussian. | `{"items":{"type":"number"},"maxItems":3,"minItems":3,"type":"array"}` | omitted |

## pvWriteCGNSWriter

Explicit-export writer for CGNS (.cgns), the CFD General Notation System read by many solvers, meshers and post-processors. It accepts structured grids, polygonal data, unstructured grids, or a multiblock containing these, and stores mesh and point/cell solution fields in one file, using HDF5 storage by default (UseHDF5) or the older ADF layout. Publication uses the semantic contract: ParaView re-reads the file and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting changes in block structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use it to hand results to CGNS-based tools; use pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter or pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter when the data only needs to round-trip through VTK.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Image and rectilinear grids are outside the documented input types; convert them to a structured or unstructured grid first.
- ParaView notes that the CGNS writer may not support ghost levels; leave GhostLevel at 0.
- Keep UseHDF5 true unless the receiving tool can only read ADF-based CGNS files.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteCSVWriter

Explicit-export writer that turns one dataset, composite dataset or table into delimited text (.csv, .txt or .tsv): one row per point, cell or table row and one column per array component, optionally with point coordinates (AddMetaData) and time columns. Use it to hand values to spreadsheets, pandas or R; mesh topology is not kept. Publication uses the table contract: Schemaxis re-reads the file and checks the row count and every input array of the written association within the export tolerance, accepting the loss of topology, coordinates and structure.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Precision defaults to 5 significant digits; raise it (17 reproduces doubles exactly) or set an export tolerance, otherwise verification usually fails.
- Verification covers one dataset or table: composite input is rejected with UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE (merge it with pvMergeBlocks first). The verifier uses the FieldAssociation, FieldDelimiter, StringDelimiter and UseStringDelimiter that ParaView holds on the created writer, so a .tsv file is checked with the tab ParaView sets for it. Author FieldAssociation as ParaView's entry text, for example "Cell Data". When it is omitted, ParaView picks (and Schemaxis reads back) the first of Point, Cell, Vertex, Edge, Row then Field Data that has arrays and tuples, which is not always the points. Only "Point Data", "Cell Data" and (for tables) "Row Data" can be verified: "Field Data", "Vertex Data" or "Edge Data" is rejected at planning with UNSUPPORTED_ASSOCIATION, and "Row Data" for a non-table input fails verification with the same fault; a delimiter longer than one character gives UNSUPPORTED_DELIMITER.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the table comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with Precision 17 and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteDataSetWriter

Explicit-export writer for the legacy VTK format (.vtk), the original single-file VTK layout still read by ParaView, VisIt, many solver converters and simple scripts. It writes one non-composite dataset of any mesh type, a table or a graph, in binary by default or ASCII (FileType). Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the file and structure, connectivity, values and storage types must match the input exactly. Prefer scene geometry or the VTK XML writers (pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter, pvWriteXMLPolyDataWriter, ...) for new work, and use this writer when a downstream tool reads only legacy .vtk files.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Composite (multiblock) inputs are rejected; merge blocks with pvMergeBlocks or use pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter.
- If exact verification of an ASCII file reports changed values, switch FileType back to Binary, which stores the values bit for bit.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteEnSightWriter

Explicit-export writer for EnSight Gold, the case format read by Ansys EnSight and many CFD post-processors: a .case index, a binary .geo geometry file and one file per point or cell array. It accepts only a single, non-composite unstructured grid; cells are grouped into EnSight parts by an integer BlockId cell array when present, otherwise everything is part 1. Publication uses the semantic contract: the case is read back and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting changes in structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter for lossless VTK storage, or pvWriteCGNSWriter / pvWriteIOSSWriter for other solver formats.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- VTK names the case file data.0.case (0 is the process number); Schemaxis finds it automatically, but keep the .case, .geo and variable files together when moving them.
- Only arrays with 1, 3, 6 or 9 components (scalar, vector, symmetric or full tensor) get a valid case-file entry, and pixel or voxel cells are skipped; remove such arrays with pvPassArrays and avoid grids built directly from image data, or verification fails.
- Field-data arrays are not stored in EnSight, while semantic verification checks them; remove field data upstream if the input carries any.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteExodusIIWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a dataset or composite dataset as an Exodus II file (.e, .g, .ex2 …), the finite-element results format of the SEACAS tools. vtkExodusIIWriter writes each leaf's cells as unstructured elements grouped into element blocks; when the input carries no Exodus metadata (it did not come from an Exodus reader) it creates one block per cell type. Publication uses the semantic contract: the file is reopened and mesh geometry and every input field are compared, while block structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type may change. Use pvWriteIOSSWriter for the IOSS path, or VTK XML output when Exodus is not required.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Without Exodus metadata VTK warns 'Attempting to proceed without metadata'; this is a warning, not a failure, and IgnoreMetaDataWarning silences it.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the semantic comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteGenericIOWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a multiblock of particle unstructured grids as one HACC GenericIO file (.gio), each block becoming one rank's data (vtkPGenericIOMultiBlockWriter). Point coordinates are written as double variables x, y, z, single-component point arrays keep their names and 3-component arrays become <name>_x, _y and _z; cells and connectivity are not stored. Schemaxis verifies it with the semantic comparison, accepting structure and storage changes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The default readback cannot set coordinate names; give readback {"operation": "pvGenericIOMultiBlockReader", "options": {"xAxis": "x", "yAxis": "y", "zAxis": "z", "PointArrayStatus": [...]}} as Schemaxis's qualification fixture does.
- If the data already have point arrays named x, y or z, the coordinates are written as xx, yy or zz instead.
- A small serial fixture passed (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json); ParaView marks the writer requires_mpi and larger or parallel data are unverified.

## pvWriteHoudiniWriter

Explicit-export writer for the ASCII Houdini geometry format (.geo, pre-version-12 PGEOMETRY V2), for taking surfaces into SideFX Houdini for effects or rendering. The input must be polygonal data; point arrays become point attributes, cell arrays primitive attributes, and triangle strips are split into triangles. Schemaxis verifies geometry only, with its own parser of the writer's exact grammar (vertices, lines, polygons, triangle strips, attribute brackets, and NPrims counting emitted triangles): points and primitives are compared with the triangulated input surface, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePOBJWriter or pvWritePSTLWriter for more widely read surface formats.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Coordinates are written with 6 significant digits (vtkHoudiniPolyDataWriter.cxx:383-386), so a zero tolerance is rejected at planning (INVALID_TOLERANCE) and publication rejects a tolerance below half a unit in the sixth digit of the largest coordinate (TOLERANCE_BELOW_WRITER_PRECISION, which reports the minimum). A tolerance of 1e-6 suits coordinates below 1; scale it with the data.
- Verification requires the geometry comparison. The Schemaxis parser reads exactly what the writer emits: vertices, lines, polygons and triangle strips (each strip triangle counts as one NPrims primitive) with attribute values in brackets ignored. A degenerate strip of fewer than 3 points corrupts the writer's own file and gives UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT; remove such cells upstream. Array selection is not needed to verify cell arrays.
- A custom readback reader is rejected for this writer; the built-in parser is always used.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with a tolerance of 1e-6 and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteHyperTreeGridWriter

Explicit-export writer for VTK's hyper tree grid XML format (.htg), which stores adaptive tree-based meshes (vtkHyperTreeGrid: a coarse grid of quadtrees or octrees) with their refinement trees, masks, coordinates and cell fields. The input must be one non-composite hyper tree grid; all its arrays are written. Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the file and tree structure, masks, coordinates and cell arrays must match exactly. Use pvWriteSerialHTGMultiBlock for a multiblock of hyper tree grids; this is also the format scene geometry chooses for hyper tree grids.

- Few tools outside VTK and ParaView read .htg; convert the data to an unstructured grid upstream when the receiver needs a conventional mesh.

## pvWriteIOSSWriter

Explicit-export writer for Exodus II (.exo) through the IOSS library, the finite-element format of Sandia's SIERRA codes, Cubit and many structural and multiphysics solvers. It accepts a dataset, a partitioned dataset or a partitioned dataset collection; every partition becomes an element block unless selectors (or, for data read by ParaView's IOSS reader, its IOSS assembly) assign partitions to blocks and sets, and a time-dependent input is exported for the one scheduled time step: Schemaxis manages TimeStepRange and TimeStepStride, because the writer otherwise loops over every input time step itself. Publication uses the semantic contract: the file is re-read and geometry plus every input point and cell field are compared, accepting loss of structure, point identity, connectivity order and storage type. Use pvWriteExodusIIWriter for ParaView's older Exodus writer and pvWriteCGNSWriter for CGNS tools.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Exodus ids start at 1. For time-dependent input, ParaView 5.13.3's IOSS writer aborts the whole run when the point global ids start at 0 or are absent (native pvbatch probe, 2026-10-12), so Schemaxis refuses such an export before writing (UNSUPPORTED_INPUT): add ids with pvGlobalPointAndCellIds and set OffsetGlobalIds true, which the probe confirmed writes the scheduled step. Static input is written either way.
- vtkIOSSWriter runs its own time loop and ignores the scheduled time (vtkIOSSWriter.cxx:285-342). A native pvbatch 5.13.3 probe found that on creation ParaView replaces the static TimeStepRange [0, 1] with the domain range [0, n-1], and a default export wrote all steps for one scheduled time. When the exported node reports two or more time steps (read from its pipeline information, so filters count too), Schemaxis sets TimeStepRange [k, k+1] and TimeStepStride 2 for the scheduled step k (probe: exactly one step, whose Point Value matched step k, for k = 0, 2 and 9); both settings are managed and cannot be authored, and a scheduled time that is not one of the input steps gives TIME_NOT_IN_INPUT. The probe did not establish the time stamp stored in the file, so do not rely on it.
- ParaView's GUI-only entity-type chooser (EntityType, which has no native command) is not exposed; select blocks and arrays with the *Selectors and *Arrays settings.
- Semantic readback compares every input point and cell array by name. Exodus stores global ids as maps rather than fields, and readers may merge arrays whose names end in X, Y and Z into one vector, so inputs carrying such arrays (for example GlobalPointIds, or Point X/Y/Z) fail verification with 'semantic readback lacks an input field'; pass only the arrays you need with pvPassArrays before exporting.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

Native binding: `IOSSWriter`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvWriteJPEGWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves image data (vtkImageData) as a JPEG (.jpg) file: 1 to 3 components of unsigned char values, compressed lossily at VTK's quality 95. Publication uses the pixels contract, comparing dimensions, components and values after re-reading, so a positive export tolerance is required (zero is rejected at planning) and pvWritePNGWriter is the choice for exact pixels.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- A tolerance of 0 is rejected at planning (INVALID_TOLERANCE) because JPEG compression changes values; choose a tolerance in the 0 to 255 value range or export PNG. Verification also requires the pixels comparison.
- VTK's writer accepts only unsigned char (8-bit) scalars (vtkJPEGWriter.cxx:219-223); other scalar types, or an image without active scalars, fail before writing with UNSUPPORTED_DATA_TYPE. Convert upstream, because Schemaxis performs no implicit conversion.
- Schemaxis manages the file name, so export 2-D images; a numbered 3-D stack needs a file pattern.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with a pixel tolerance of 3 and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

Native binding: `JPEGWriter`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvWriteJSONImageWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a uniform image (vtkImageData) node as a JSON document listing the image dimensions, origin, spacing and the values of its point arrays, for web or scripting tools rather than for re-reading in ParaView. Use it as an export `writer` with comparison "pixels": Schemaxis then parses the JSON itself and checks dimensions, origin, spacing and exactly the arrays the writer emits against the source image: one-component point arrays other than vtkValidPointMask, narrowed by ArrayName and Slice, with null where vtkValidPointMask is 0. The input must be non-composite image data; resample other datasets to an image first. For standard raster formats use pvWritePNGWriter, pvWriteTIFFWriter or pvWriteMetaImageWriter.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ArrayName and Slice are honoured by the verifier: ArrayName must name a one-component point array (otherwise nothing is written and verification fails), and Slice must be -1 or below the image depth (a larger Slice is rejected with INVALID_SLICE before writing, because VTK does not bound-check it). Vector arrays and vtkValidPointMask are never written.
- The writer prints values, origin and spacing with 6 significant digits (VTK vtkVariant::ToString precision 6), so floating-point data usually needs a positive tolerance.
- Only pixels comparison is accepted and a custom readback reader is rejected for this writer.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

Native binding: `JSONImageWriter`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## pvWriteMetaImageWriter

Explicit-export writer for MetaImage (.mhd): a short text header (dimensions, spacing, element type) plus a separate binary data file, the format read by ITK-based medical-imaging and segmentation tools. The input must be one non-composite vtkImageData; VTK writes the image scalars and compresses the data file by default. Schemaxis publishes it under the pixels contract: the file is read back and dimensions, component count and scalar values are compared, while coordinates and other fields are accepted as lost. Use pvWriteTIFFWriter or pvWritePNGWriter for 2-D raster interchange, or automatic VTK XML image output (.vti) to keep all arrays.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only the image scalars are carried; make the array you need the active point scalars, or export VTK XML image data when several arrays matter.
- Keep the header and its data file together when moving the result; the header refers to the data file by name.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteOpenVDBWriter

Explicit-export writer for OpenVDB (.vdb), the sparse volume format used by Houdini, Blender and film-style renderers. It accepts non-composite image data (volumes) or point sets (meshes or point clouds handled through their points); with EnableColoring it adds a colour channel, and with EnableAlpha an alpha channel, computed from a lookup table supplied through the export's LookupTable resource. The declared publication uses the exact contract, comparing ParaView's readback of the .vdb with the input. Use it to send simulation volumes to rendering tools; keep pvWriteXMLImageDataWriter for lossless analysis data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- An earlier Schemaxis catalogue check of this writer failed because the readback differed from the input; expect exact verification to fail and set a comparison and accepted losses that match what VDB keeps.
- EnableColoring needs a lookup table connected through resources (LookupTable) and the array to map named in ColorArrayName; otherwise no colour channel can be computed.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) failed on a small serial fixture with default options: the readback differed from the input; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the file in the receiving tool.

## pvWritePNGWriter

Explicit-export writer that stores image data (vtkImageData) as PNG, a lossless raster format holding 1 to 4 components of unsigned char (8-bit) or unsigned short (16-bit) values. It suits masks, label images and already-quantized images, not floating-point simulation fields; this writes data values, unlike a rendered scene image. Publication uses the pixels contract: the PNG is read back and its dimensions, components and values are compared with the input scalars. Use pvWriteTIFFWriter for 32-bit float data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Float or double arrays are not supported; rescale and convert them to 8- or 16-bit integers upstream, because Schemaxis performs no implicit conversion.
- Natively a 3-D image can be written as a numbered slice stack through a file pattern, but Schemaxis manages the file name, so export 2-D images.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWritePOBJWriter

Explicit-export writer for Wavefront OBJ (.obj), a plain-text surface format read by almost every 3-D modelling, rendering and visualization tool. It writes the points, lines, triangles and polygons of polygonal data plus point normals and texture coordinates when present; solution fields are not stored. TextureFileName additionally writes a material (.mtl) file that refers to an existing texture image. Publication uses the geometry contract: the file is read back and the triangulated surface is compared, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePSTLWriter for triangle-only CAD or 3-D printing exchange, and VTK XML writers when fields matter.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Scalar and vector fields (pressure, velocity, ...) are lost; export a VTK XML format when the receiver needs them.
- TextureFileName is written into the .mtl as given and the image is not copied into the output folder; use a path that still resolves where the OBJ will be opened.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with a tolerance of 1e-6 and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWritePPLYWriter

Explicit-export writer for Stanford PLY (.ply): polygonal surface geometry (points and polygons) for mesh, 3-D printing and point-cloud tools, binary by default (FileType). It accepts polygonal data only, so extract a surface first (pvExtractSurface). Field arrays are not carried, except optional per-point or per-cell RGB(A) colours written when EnableColoring is true, ColorArrayName names the array and a lookup-table resource is attached to the export. Publication uses the geometry contract: Schemaxis re-reads the file with ParaView's PLY reader and compares the triangulated surface within the tolerance.

- Colours need all three: EnableColoring true, ColorArrayName and a LookupTable resource in the export's resources; otherwise the writer writes geometry only.

## pvWritePSTLWriter

Explicit-export writer for STL (.stl), the triangle-only surface format used by 3-D printing, CAD and meshing tools (for example as snappyHexMesh geometry). It writes binary STL by default or ASCII with FileType; only triangles are stored, with no units or fields. Publication uses the geometry contract: the file is re-read and its triangles are compared with the triangulated input surface within the tolerance, accepting loss of fields, point identity, interior cells and structure. Use pvWritePOBJWriter to keep polygons and normals, or pvWritePPLYWriter for per-vertex attributes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Lines and vertex cells are not written to STL, so an input that contains them fails the geometry verification (Schemaxis compares the triangulated input, which keeps them); extract the surface (pvExtractSurface) and keep only polygons before exporting. Polygons with more than three vertices are triangulated by vtkSTLWriter itself; the ParaView help text about writing only their first three vertices is out of date.
- Binary STL stores coordinates as 32-bit floats; give a small tolerance (the guide's example uses 0.000001) when the input uses double precision.
- STL carries no length unit; check millimetres versus metres in the receiving tool.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with a tolerance of 1e-6 and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteSerialHTGMultiBlock

Explicit-export writer that saves a multiblock dataset whose blocks are hyper tree grids as a VTK multiblock file (.vtm) plus one .htg file per block in a data/ subfolder. ParaView marks its input as composite-only (the input contract records composite as "required"): the node must output a multiblock of hyper tree grids. ## pvWriteTIFFWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves image data (vtkImageData) as TIFF. vtkTIFFWriter accepts unsigned char, unsigned short or float scalars, so unlike PNG it can store 32-bit floating-point fields such as a sampled temperature image. Scalars selects which point array becomes the image values. Publication uses the pixels contract: the TIFF is read back and dimensions, components and values are compared; coordinates and other arrays are not preserved.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Double-precision and other integer types are rejected by the native writer; convert the array to float (or 8/16-bit unsigned) upstream.
- Name the array in Scalars; otherwise ParaView decides which array is written.

## pvWriteVTKHDFWriter

Explicit-export writer for VTKHDF (.vtkhdf), VTK's HDF5-based single-file format, suited to large meshes and to parallel or partial reading. ## pvWriteXMLImageDataWriter

Explicit-export writer for VTK XML image data (.vti): a uniform grid (origin, spacing, dimensions, direction) with all point, cell and field arrays, stored losslessly in one file. ## pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter

Explicit-export writer for VTK XML multiblock data (.vtm): an index describing the block tree (names and nesting) plus one VTK XML file per leaf dataset in a data/ subfolder, keeping every array. ## pvWriteXMLPHyperTreeGridWriter

Parallel-layout writer for hyper tree grids: a .phtg summary file that lists one .htg piece per process. Schemaxis runs explicit exports serially, so the result is one piece; choosing a parallel writer does not launch MPI. Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the summary and trees, masks and cell arrays must match exactly. Prefer pvWriteHyperTreeGridWriter, which writes the same data as one self-contained .htg file.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ParaView 5.13.3 completes the write (a .phtg summary plus a piece .htg file), but its XMLPHyperTreeGridReader crashes with a segmentation fault when it opens the .phtg, while the HyperTreeGridReader (pvHyperTreeGridReader), which ParaView picks for a piece .htg, reads the piece. Schemaxis verifies an export by reading it back, so exporting through this writer crashes the native process at readback (a bounded native probe, 2026-10-12, reproduced it in a separate process from the write, opening the file with OpenDataFile as publish does without a readback override); use pvWriteHyperTreeGridWriter unless you specifically need the .phtg layout.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) failed on a small serial fixture with WriteTimeValue false and the other options at their defaults: ParaView crashed with a segmentation fault; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the file in the receiving tool.

## pvWriteXMLPVDWriter

Explicit-export writer for ParaView's PVD format: a small XML .pvd index plus the VTK XML piece file(s) it references (type chosen from the data, e.g. .vtu or .vtp), written into a subdirectory named after the file, for one time step. It accepts a single non-composite dataset or table. Publication uses the exact contract: the .pvd is reopened and structure, connectivity, values and storage types must match the input. Choose it when the recipient expects a .pvd collection; otherwise a single-file pvWriteXML…Writer is simpler.

- Keep the .pvd and its subdirectory together; the index refers to the piece files by relative path.

## pvWriteXMLPartitionedDataSetCollectionWriter

Explicit-export writer for VTK XML partitioned dataset collections (.vtpc): an index plus one VTK XML file per partition in a data/ subfolder, keeping the collection's partitioned datasets, names, data assembly and arrays. Scene geometry uses the same format automatically for collections (for example multi-region readers' output); choose this writer for explicit storage settings or block selection. Publication uses the exact contract: ParaView re-reads the .vtpc and the partitions, names, assembly and arrays must match exactly. Use pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter for multiblock data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the exact comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node. ChooseBlocksToWrite true is rejected at planning (BLOCK_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because no comparison accepts missing blocks; extract the blocks to keep with pvExtractBlock and export that node.
- Keep the .vtpc and its data/ folder together; the index refers to the pieces by relative path.

## pvWriteXMLPolyDataWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a polygonal (vtkPolyData) node, such as a slice, contour, extracted surface, lines or points, as a VTK XML PolyData file (.vtp) with its geometry, connectivity and point, cell and field arrays. Schemaxis reopens the file and requires an exact match of structure, connectivity, values and storage types, so the .vtp is a lossless copy of the node. Automatic geometry output already writes .vtp for polydata; choose this writer when you need to control the encoding (DataMode, CompressorType) or want an export receipt. Use pvWriteXMLUnstructuredGridWriter for volume meshes and pvWriteXMLMultiBlockDataWriter for composite data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The input must be one non-composite polydata; merge or extract a block from multiblock data first, or the input-domain check rejects the export.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the exact comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.
- Schemaxis switches off the writer's TimeValue field array unless you author it, so the exact comparison sees only the node's own arrays; the selected time is kept in the export receipt.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteXMLRectilinearGridWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a rectilinear grid (vtkRectilinearGrid: a structured grid with independent, possibly non-uniform, coordinate arrays along x, y and z) as a VTK XML RectilinearGrid file (.vtr), keeping the extent, the three coordinate arrays and all point, cell and field arrays. Schemaxis verifies the reopened file with an exact comparison. Automatic geometry output already writes .vtr for this type; use this writer to control encoding or to get an explicit export receipt. For uniform spacing the data are usually image data (pvWriteXMLImageDataWriter); for curvilinear grids use pvWriteXMLStructuredGridWriter.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only a single non-composite rectilinear grid is accepted; other grid types are rejected by the input-domain check rather than converted.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the exact comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.
- Schemaxis switches off the writer's TimeValue field array unless you author it, so the exact comparison sees only the node's own arrays; the selected time is kept in the export receipt.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with default options; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvWriteXMLTableWriter

Explicit-export writer that saves a table (vtkTable), such as probe-over-line, integration or statistics results, as a VTK XML Table file (.vtt) that keeps every column with its name, type and component count. Unlike pvWriteCSVWriter it is binary-capable and lossless, and Schemaxis verifies the reopened file with an exact comparison. Automatic geometry output already writes .vtt for tables; choose this writer for encoding control or an explicit export receipt. The input must be a single table, not a dataset with point or cell data.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Datasets (meshes) are rejected; convert them to a table upstream if you need tabular output.
- Choose CSV (pvWriteCSVWriter) instead when the file must be read by spreadsheets or scripts that do not understand VTK XML.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the exact comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node.

## pvWriteXMLUniformGridAMRWriter

Explicit-export writer for adaptive-mesh-refinement data (vtkUniformGridAMR, overlapping or non-overlapping): it writes a .vthb index file plus one VTK XML image file per AMR block in a companion folder, keeping levels, refinement ratios, block extents and all arrays. Schemaxis reopens the set (asking the reader for all levels) and requires an exact match. Automatic geometry already writes .vthb for overlapping AMR; choose this writer for encoding or header-size control or an explicit export receipt. pvWriteXMLHierarchicalBoxDataWriter is the deprecated name of the same format.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Keep the .vthb file and its data folder together; the index refers to the block files by relative path.
- ChooseArraysToWrite true is rejected at planning (ARRAY_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because the exact comparison needs every input array in the file; filter arrays with pvPassArrays and export that node. ChooseBlocksToWrite true is rejected at planning (BLOCK_SELECTION_UNVERIFIABLE) because no comparison accepts missing blocks; extract the blocks to keep with pvExtractBlock and export that node.
- Schemaxis switches off the writer's TimeValue field array unless you author WriteTimeValue, so the exact comparison sees only the node's own arrays; the selected time is kept in the export receipt.
- An earlier catalogue run (verification/2026-09-16-catalogue-expansion.json, writerQualification) passed only on a small serial fixture with WriteTimeValue false and the other options at their defaults; no current native acceptance check is recorded, so verify the export on representative data.

## pvXDMFReader

Reads XDMF 2 files (.xmf/.xdmf): XML metadata with heavy arrays in HDF5. The output is the file's grid type (unstructured, structured or rectilinear) or a multiblock when it has several grids. Several file names form a file series read as time steps. Selections choose which grids, sets and point or cell arrays are loaded, and Stride subsamples structured grids. It is a distributed reader. pvXdmf3ReaderT and pvXdmf3ReaderS read XDMF 3 files.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The HDF5 file must stay where the XML references it, usually beside the .xmf file.
- Array, grid and set selections start from ParaView's choice; list them when later steps depend on particular names.
- Schemaxis generates this reader binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check with a sample file of this format.

## pvXMLHierarchicalBoxDatareader

Reads VTK XML hierarchical-box AMR files (.vthb, .vth) in the version 1.0 or older layout: a summary file referring to vtkUniformGrid pieces at several refinement levels, read as an overlapping AMR dataset. For the newer layout use pvXMLUniformGridAMRReader, which also offers array selection and a level limit. Several summary files form a time series.

## pvYieldCriteria

Evaluates yield criteria of selected symmetric stress tensors from their principal values σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3: Tresca as |σ3 − σ1| and von Mises as √(((σ1 − σ2)² + (σ2 − σ3)² + (σ1 − σ3)²) / 2), stored as <name> - Tresca Criterion and <name> - Von Mises Criterion in the tensor's units. The Principal Stress choice also keeps the principal value and direction arrays. Use it in structural post-processing to compare stress states with a material's yield strength. Tensor requirements match pvTensorPrincipalInvariants (6 components XX, YY, ZZ, XY, YZ, XZ, or 3 named XX, YY, XY).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The Tresca value here is the full principal-stress difference, twice the maximum shear stress; compare it with the yield strength, not the shear yield strength.
- If no criterion is selected the input passes through unchanged.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## pvYoungsMaterialInterface

Reconstructs sharp material interfaces in mixed cells of Eulerian or ALE multi-material simulations (e.g. CTH or other volume-of-fluid output) with Youngs' method: in each cell the material is bounded by a plane perpendicular to its interface normal, placed so the cut volume matches the cell's volume fraction. Input is a composite dataset with one cell-centred volume fraction array per material and, ideally, a 3-component cell normal array per material. Output is a multiblock with one block per material (in VolumeFractionArrays order) holding the interface polygons or, with FillMaterial (ParaView default), the material's volume.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Without a normal array for a material, VTK uses the +x direction, so interfaces come out as planes perpendicular to x; supply normals (e.g. from the volume-fraction gradient).
- AxisSymetric is true by ParaView default and treats 2-D meshes as axisymmetric (volumes of revolution); set it false for planar 2-D data.
- Only 2-D and 3-D cells are processed and input must be composite (e.g. multiblock); wrap a single mesh with pvGroupDatasets first.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

Native binding: `YoungsMaterialInterface`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

Coverage: `{"defaults":"native defaults for omitted options","gaps":{},"origin":"generated","output":"native inspection required; explicit output-port selection available","outputPorts":null,"qualification":"not-run"}`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Input` | one node | yes | `data` |

Input `Input` contract: `{"compatibility":"native-domain-checked","composite":null,"cost":{"basis":"no benchmark","conversion":"none inserted","rating":"unknown"},"nativeTypes":["vtkCompositeDataSet"],"requirements":{},"traits":{"contiguity":"unknown","indexing":"unknown","iteration":"unknown"}}`.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AxisSymetric` | For 2-D cells, treats the mesh as an axisymmetric section (volume of revolution about the axis) when placing interfaces, so cut positions honour revolved volumes rather than planar areas. It has no effect on 3-D cells. Native name keeps ParaView's spelling. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `FillMaterial` | When true, each material block contains the material's volume: pure cells whole plus the material side of every cut mixed cell. When false, only the interface itself is output (polygons in 3-D, lines in 2-D) and pure cells are omitted. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `InverseNormal` | Flips the sign of every material normal before the interface is placed, which moves the material to the other side of its interface plane. Use it when the supplied normals point out of the material (e.g. a plain volume-fraction gradient points into it). | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `NormalArrays` | Assigns an interface-normal cell array to materials, as a flat list of pairs [volume-fraction array, normal array, volume-fraction array, normal array, …]. Each normal array is a 3-component cell array giving the interface orientation for that material; materials without one get a degenerate normal replaced by +x. | `{"items":{"type":"string"},"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `OnionPeel` | When true, materials are processed in order within each cell and all use the first material's normal, like layers of an onion, which keeps nested interfaces parallel and avoids overlaps in cells with three or more materials. When false, each material uses its own normal. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `OrderingArrays` | Assigns an ordering cell array to materials, as a flat list of pairs [volume-fraction array, ordering array, …]. In each cell, materials are processed in ascending order of their ordering value (descending with ReverseMaterialOrder), which matters with OnionPeel. Materials without one have ordering 0 and keep their VolumeFractionArrays order. | `{"items":{"type":"string"},"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `ReverseMaterialOrder` | Reverses the order in which materials are processed in each cell (descending ordering value instead of ascending, or reverse list order without ordering arrays). With OnionPeel this changes which material forms the inner layer. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `UseFractionAsDistance` | When true, the volume-fraction value is used directly as the distance of the interface plane from the cell origin along the normal, instead of solving for the plane that matches the volume fraction; the fraction range thresholds are then bypassed. Use it only when the arrays store plane distances (e.g. level-set style data). | `{"type":"boolean"}` | omitted |
| `VolumeFractionArrays` | Names of the cell-centred volume-fraction arrays (values 0 to 1), one per material; the list order is the material index and the order of the output blocks. Blocks lacking an array simply contribute nothing for that material. | `{"items":{"type":"string"},"type":"array"}` | omitted |
| `VolumeFractionRange` | Thresholds [min, max] on a material's volume fraction in a cell: at or below min the cell is treated as empty of that material, at or above max as full (copied whole only when FillMaterial is true), and in between an interface is reconstructed. Narrowing the range removes slivers from nearly pure cells. | `{"items":{"maximum":1.0,"minimum":0.0,"type":"number"},"maxItems":2,"minItems":2,"type":"array"}` | omitted |

- `NormalArrays` requires complete groups of 2 values.
- `OrderingArrays` requires complete groups of 2 values.

## pva3DText

Creates polygonal (filled outline) geometry spelling Text in a vector font, lying in the x-y plane with the text starting near the origin and characters about one unit tall. It is real geometry, so it can be transformed, clipped or exported, unlike a screen-space text annotation. Use it to label parts of a 3-D scene.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Only printable ASCII characters and "\n" line breaks are supported.
- Scale and place the text with a transform; the source has no size or position options.
- Schemaxis generates this source from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for it, so inspect the output before relying on it.

## pvglTFReader

Reads a glTF 2.0 asset (.gltf with external buffers, or binary .glb) into a multiblock dataset of polydata for one scene, with skinning, morph targets and enabled animations applied to the geometry when ApplyDeformationsToGeometry is true. Animations become time steps sampled at Framerate. Materials and textures are not applied. Use it to bring 3-D models or animated scenes into a pipeline; for static CAD surfaces pvWavefrontOBJReader or readSTL are simpler.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- No animation is enabled by default (glTF does not define which should play); list them in AnimationStatus to get time steps.
- glTF coordinates are metres by specification, but scenes from other tools may not follow that; nothing is converted.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this reader, so inspect the output blocks, arrays and time steps on your own files before relying on it.

## pvopenPMDReader

Reads an openPMD particle-mesh data series (plasma and accelerator simulations such as WarpX or PIConGPU) through a .pmd file: a text file whose first line is the openPMD file pattern, e.g. "data_%T.h5", resolved next to the .pmd file. - The reader needs the openpmd_api Python module inside ParaView's Python; without it nothing is read.
- Point FileName at the .pmd pattern file, not at an individual HDF5 or ADIOS iteration file.
- Schemaxis generates this binding from ParaView's catalogue; it has not run a native acceptance check for this operation.

## reflect

Mirrors the input across an axis-aligned plane and outputs an unstructured grid (a composite input gives a multiblock of unstructured grids) holding the mirrored copy, plus the original when copyInput is true. Use it to rebuild a full model from a half- or quarter-symmetry simulation, or to mirror a part for display. The plane is x, y or z = centre (Schemaxis default plane X at 0) or one face of the input's bounding box (X Min to Z Max). Vector and tensor arrays such as velocity are mirrored with the geometry because ParaView's FlipAllInputArrays stays at its default (on); scalars are copied unchanged.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The two halves are appended, not merged: points on the mirror plane are duplicated and the halves are not connected. Run cleanGrid afterwards when connectivity matters, e.g. before surface, connectivity or point-based gradients.
- Image data, rectilinear and structured grids become an unstructured grid, which can need much more memory than the input.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Reflect`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |

## resample

Samples the arrays of the input node (port input, native SourceDataArrays) at the points of the mesh node (port mesh, native DestinationMesh). The result has the mesh's geometry with the input's point and cell values interpolated to its points and a vtkValidPointMask array; with passPointArrays (Schemaxis default true) the mesh's own point arrays are kept too. Use it to compare or combine results on a common mesh, e.g. map a CFD field onto a measurement or structural mesh; pvResampleWithDataset exposes the remaining native settings.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The ports are easily swapped: input supplies the values, mesh supplies the geometry.
- Mesh points outside the input get vtkValidPointMask 0 and unusable values; threshold on the mask before statistics.

## shrink

Moves the points of every cell towards that cell's centroid (the average of its points) so that cells separate from their neighbours, and outputs an unstructured grid in which no point is shared between cells. It is a mesh-inspection aid that reveals cell shapes, sizes and gaps inside a volume or surface mesh; point and cell arrays travel with the cells. factor is the fraction of each cell's size kept (Schemaxis default 0.8; ParaView's own default is 0.5).

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Every shared point is duplicated once per cell, so point count and memory grow several-fold on volume meshes; shrink a slice, surface or extracted subset of a large mesh instead.
- Do not measure or integrate the result: shrinking scales each cell's area by factor squared and its volume by factor cubed.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default factor; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Shrink`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `factor` | The value of this property determines how far the points will move. A value of 0 positions the points at the centroid of the cell. A value of 1 leaves them at their original positions. | `{"type":"number","minimum":0,"maximum":1}` | `0.8` |


## slice

Cuts the input with one infinite plane through origin, perpendicular to normal, and returns polygonal data: a surface from a volume mesh, lines from a surface. Point arrays are interpolated onto the cut and cell arrays are copied from the cell each polygon came from, so cell-centred CFD fields appear piecewise constant. Use it for cross-sections of 3-D fields; use clip to keep one side of a volume, contour for an isosurface, probeLine for a 1-D profile, and pvSlice for several parallel offsets or other cut shapes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- origin defaults to [0, 0, 0], not to the centre of your data as in the ParaView GUI. A plane that misses the data gives empty geometry, which Schemaxis reports as EMPTY_GEOMETRY; set origin inside the dataset bounds.
- Hyper tree grid input is refused with INPUT_TRAIT_MISMATCH (recovery: use pvSlice): this operation sets only ParaView's SliceType, whereas a hyper tree grid is cut by the separate HyperTreeGridImplicitFunction, so origin and normal would have no effect on it.
- Native acceptance (examples/schemaxis/acceptance.py) checks that slices lie on the requested plane and that integrals over a wavelet slice match analytic values; crinkle output and real CFD meshes are not separately checked.

Native binding: `Slice`. Output kind: `["data"]`.
