## smooth

Applies Laplacian smoothing to a polygonal surface: each iteration moves every point a small step towards the average of its connected neighbours. The output is polygonal data with the same points and connectivity at smoother positions, and arrays are passed unchanged. Use it to reduce faceting or noise on scanned, marching-cubes or STL surfaces before rendering or curvature. Input must be vtkPolyData; run surface first on volume meshes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Laplacian smoothing shrinks surfaces and rounds sharp features; compare volumes or key dimensions with the input before measuring the result.
- VTK's relaxation factor (0.01) is not exposed, so 20 iterations move points only slightly; raise iterations for stronger smoothing.
- Feature edges are not protected and open boundaries are smoothed too (VTK defaults: feature-edge smoothing off, boundary smoothing on); neither smooth nor pvSmooth exposes these switches.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a sphere with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Smooth`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |

Input `input` contract: `{"compatibility":"native-domain-checked","composite":null,"cost":{"basis":"no benchmark","conversion":"none inserted","rating":"unknown"},"nativeTypes":["vtkPolyData"],"requirements":{},"traits":{"contiguity":"unknown","indexing":"unknown","iteration":"unknown"}}`.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `iterations` | This property sets the maximum number of smoothing iterations to perform. More iterations produce better smoothing. | `{"type":"integer","minimum":0}` | `20` |
| `convergence` | The value of this property limits the maximum motion of any point. It is expressed as a fraction of the length of the diagonal of the bounding box of the input dataset. If the maximum point motion during a smoothing iteration is less than the value of this property, the smoothing operation terminates. | `{"type":"number","minimum":0}` | `0` |


## sphere

Creates a triangulated polygonal sphere (vtkPolyData with point normals) of given radius about centre, with its poles on the z axis. resolution sets the number of longitude divisions around z (Schemaxis default 24, ParaView's own default 8); latitude divisions are fixed at 24 by Schemaxis. Use it as a marker, a target mesh for resample, a seed surface for streamTracer or simple test geometry; its coordinates are in the units of the data it is combined with.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Latitude resolution (PhiResolution) is fixed at 24, so a very high resolution gives long thin facets; use pvSphere to set ThetaResolution and PhiResolution together or to make a partial sphere.
- The facets lie inside the true sphere, so the surface area and enclosed volume are slightly smaller than the analytic values, noticeably so at low resolution.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, with the default options; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Sphere`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

Inputs: none.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `centre` | This property specifies the 3D coordinates for the center of the sphere. | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"number"},"minItems":3,"maxItems":3}` | `[0,0,0]` |
| `radius` | This property specifies the radius of the sphere. | `{"type":"number","minimum":0,"exclusiveMinimum":true}` | `1` |
| `resolution` | The value of this property represents the number of divisions between Start Theta and End Theta around the sphere. (See the Start Theta and End Theta properties.) The theta divisions are similar to longitude lines on the earth. The higher the resolution, the closer the approximation will come to a sphere, and the more polygons there will be. | `{"type":"integer","minimum":3}` | `24` |


## streamTracer

Integrates streamlines of a steady vector field from the points of a separate seed dataset and returns polygonal data made of polylines. Connect the flow dataset to input and any point-producing node (line, sphere, a slice) to seed; every seed point starts a trace. Input point arrays are interpolated onto the lines and ParaView adds IntegrationTime, Vorticity, Rotation and AngularVelocity point arrays and a ReasonForTermination cell array. Point vectors are interpolated along the trace. A cell vector array (association CELLS) is traced as constant within each cell, but ParaView's input domain also requires some three-component point array on the input, so a cell-only input fails INPUT_DOMAIN_MISMATCH at update. Convert cell-centred CFD velocity with cellToPoint for the usual smooth traces. The integrator stays at ParaView's Runge-Kutta 4-5 with step lengths in cell lengths. Use pvStreamTracerWithCustomSource to change the integrator, step unit or terminal speed, and pvStreamTracer for ParaView's built-in seed shapes.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- These are instantaneous streamlines at the selected time, not pathlines or particle tracks through changing timesteps.
- maximumLength (Schemaxis default 20) is an absolute arc length in dataset units, not a fraction of the domain; scale it to your geometry, or lines in a large domain stop early.
- Empty or truncated lines usually mean seeds outside the flow cells, the wrong vector array, or speed below ParaView's terminal speed (1e-12). ReasonForTermination tells why each line stopped: 1 left the domain, 4 maximum length, 5 maximum steps, 6 terminal speed.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, tracing a uniform analytic velocity from a line of seeds; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `StreamTracerWithCustomSource`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |
| `seed` | one node | yes | `data` |

| `direction` | FORWARD follows the vector orientation, BACKWARD goes against it, and BOTH traces from each seed in both directions. | `{"type":"enum","values":["FORWARD","BACKWARD","BOTH"]}` | `"FORWARD"` |
| `maximumLength` | Upper limit on the arc length of each integrated trajectory. Integration may stop earlier at a dataset boundary, low speed or the step limit. | `{"type":"number","minimum":0,"exclusiveMinimum":true}` | `20` |

## surface

Extracts the outer boundary surface of any dataset as polygonal data: the exterior faces of volume cells plus any 2-D, line and vertex cells already present. Use it to turn a volume mesh into a surface for rendering, normals, featureEdges, decimate or surface export, or to see the whole boundary of a CFD domain (walls, inlets and outlets together). Cell arrays are copied from the adjacent cell to each face and point arrays are passed; nothing is interpolated.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Interior faces are removed, so use slice or clip to see inside. Composite data is surfaced block by block, so faces between blocks remain.
- Cell values on the surface are those of the adjacent volume cell, not boundary-condition values; for OpenFOAM patch values select the patch regions in foam instead.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on point data derived from the wavelet; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `ExtractSurface`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## temporalStatistics

Computes, for every point and cell array of a time-dependent input, its average, minimum, maximum and population standard deviation over all input time steps, which the filter requests itself. The output has the input's type and geometry, no time, and arrays named <name>_average, <name>_minimum, <name>_maximum and <name>_stddev (other arrays are not kept). Every step is weighted equally regardless of time spacing, so this is not a time integral. Schemaxis enables all four statistics by default; use pvTemporalStatistics only if you want the generated binding with native option names.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Unequal time steps bias the average; resample time first if the spacing varies.
- Every time step is read and processed, which can take long on large series; restrict the input time range first.
- The mesh must keep the same points and cells over time; on changing meshes the statistics are meaningless.

Native binding: `TemporalStatistics`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## threshold

Keeps the cells of a mesh whose selected point or cell scalar lies inside the inclusive range [lower, upper], producing an unstructured grid. Schemaxis fixes ParaView's ThresholdMethod to Between, requires all three options, checks that lower does not exceed upper and that the named array exists with the stated association. Use it to isolate a region such as hot gas or a recirculation zone; use pvThreshold for inverted, one-sided or component-wise tests.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- For point arrays ParaView's AllScalars default (true) applies: a cell is kept only if all of its points are in range, which shrinks the region compared with a cell-array threshold.
- Cells are kept whole, so the boundary is stepped; use contour or clip for a smooth iso-boundary.

Native binding: `Threshold`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |

## transform

Applies a linear transform to the point coordinates: scale, then rotation, then translation, all about the coordinate origin [0, 0, 0]. Vectors and normals are transformed with the geometry (every three-component array while allVectors is true). Polygonal, unstructured and structured grids keep their type; image data and rectilinear grids become an explicit-point dataset. Use it to position, orient or rescale geometry, e.g. scale [0.001, 0.001, 0.001] to convert millimetre coordinates to metres.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Rotation and scaling act about the origin, not the dataset centre, so an object away from the origin also moves. Translate it to the origin first, or use pvTransform with RotateAroundOriginTransform.
- Transformed vector arrays are rotated and scaled too: a millimetre-to-metre scale also multiplies velocity-like vectors by 0.001. Field values are never unit-converted.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, translating a sphere by [1, 2, 3]; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Transform`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

| Input port | Multiplicity | Required | Kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `input` | one node | yes | `data` |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `rotate` | Rotation angles in degrees about the x, y and z axes through the origin [0, 0, 0]. vtkPVTransform composes RotateZ, RotateX, RotateY, so the points are turned about y first, then x, then z (fixed axes), after scaling and before translation. Positive angles follow the right-hand rule about each positive axis. | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"number"},"minItems":3,"maxItems":3}` | `[0,0,0]` |
| `scale` | Factors [sx, sy, sz] multiplying the x, y and z coordinates about the origin, applied before rotation and translation. Equal factors change size or units, e.g. [0.001, 0.001, 0.001] for millimetres to metres; unequal factors stretch the geometry. | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"number"},"minItems":3,"maxItems":3}` | `[1,1,1]` |
| `allVectors` | If off, only Vectors and Normals will be transformed. If on, all three-component data arrays (considered as 3D vectors) will be transformed. All other arrays won't be flipped and will only be copied. | `{"type":"boolean"}` | `true` |


## triangulate

Converts polygonal data so that every polygon and triangle strip becomes triangles and polylines become single line segments; vertices are kept. The output is vtkPolyData on the same points, with cell values copied from each parent cell. Use it before operations or exports that need triangles, such as decimate or STL output. It accepts only polygonal input: run surface first for volume data, or use pvTetrahedralize to split volume cells into tetrahedra.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The cell count grows (a quadrilateral becomes two triangles) and cell values are repeated on each piece, so per-cell counts and cell-based statistics change, while point data is unaffected.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a wavelet slice; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Triangulate`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## tube

Builds a polygonal tube of constant radius around each line or polyline of polygonal input, typically streamlines from streamTracer, so that thin lines become visible shaded geometry in images and exports. The output is vtkPolyData, and input point arrays are carried onto the tube surface so it can be coloured by the same fields. Schemaxis assigns radius 0.1, 12 sides and capped ends; ParaView's radius variation stays off, so use pvTube for tubes whose radius follows a scalar or vector.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- radius is an absolute length in dataset units: 0.1 vanishes on a 100 m domain and swamps a 1 mm one. ParaView's GUI starts from 1% of the input extent, a reasonable first choice.
- Lines with repeated consecutive points are not tubed; run clean first if segments are missing.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on streamlines of a uniform analytic field; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `Tube`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## warpScalar

Displaces each point along a direction by scale times a point scalar (new position = point + scale x value x direction), turning a field on a flat surface into a relief or carpet plot, or moving a surface by a normal displacement. With useNormal true (Schemaxis default) every point moves along the same normal (default z+); with useNormal false the input's point normals are used when present. The output keeps the input type, except that image data and rectilinear grids become a structured grid; all arrays are carried along.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The warp distance is in dataset units: choose scale so that the field range times scale is a modest fraction of the geometry size, otherwise the relief dwarfs or hides the shape.
- Schemaxis normalizes normal, so its length does not change the displacement; express any magnification through scale.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a planar slice with a linear field; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

Native binding: `WarpByScalar`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

## warpVector

Moves every point by scale times a three-component point vector (new position = point + scale x vector), typically to show a structural displacement field or exaggerate a deformation mode. The output keeps the input type (image data and rectilinear grids become structured grids) and carries all arrays. With scale 1 and a displacement in the same length units as the coordinates the result is the true deformed shape; warping by a velocity is only a visual distortion.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- The displacement must be in the coordinate units: a displacement in millimetres on a mesh in metres needs scale 0.001 for the true shape.
- Large scales can fold or invert cells; do not compute volumes or mesh quality on an exaggerated warp.
- Schemaxis's serial native acceptance run (examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json) executes this operation once, on a wavelet with a uniform vector field and scale 0.25; it does not check this operation's output values, so inspect the result on your own data.

## wavelet

Creates a synthetic uniform image (vtkImageData) whose point array RTData combines a Gaussian peak of height maximum with sinusoidal terms along x, y and z. With the Schemaxis defaults it is a 21 x 21 x 21-point grid with unit spacing spanning -10 to 10 on each axis. Use it as a self-contained input to try slice, contour, clip, streamTracer or scene settings without a real case; its values have no physical meaning or units.

Common mistakes and assumptions:

- Each extent minimum must be smaller than its maximum, so the curated wavelet cannot produce a 2-D image; use pvWavelet for planar or subsampled images and to change frequencies, amplitudes or the Gaussian width.
- RTData is a scalar; derive test vectors with calculator (e.g. iHat), as the native acceptance example examples/schemaxis/extended-coverage.json does before its analytic integral checks.

Native binding: `Wavelet`. Output kind: `["data"]`.

Inputs: none.

| Option | Meaning | Type / constraints | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `extent` | The six values in this property indicate the X, Y, and Z extent of the output data. The first two values represent the minimum and maximum X indices, the next two are the minimum and maximum Y indices, and the last two are the minimum and maximum Z indices. | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"integer"},"minItems":6,"maxItems":6}` | `[-10,10,-10,10,-10,10]` |
| `centre` | Centre of the Gaussian and origin of the wave coordinates, in grid-index units: for each point, x, y and z are the offsets of its grid index from Center, divided by the extent width on that axis, and the Gaussian depends on their length r. It is not in physical units. ParaView's own text refers to "the equation" it prints, which multiplies the terms; the filter adds them to the Gaussian. | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"number"},"minItems":3,"maxItems":3}` | `[0,0,0]` |
| `maximum` | Height of the Gaussian term of RTData at centre. It is not the maximum of the output: sine and cosine terms (ParaView amplitudes 10, 18 and 5) are added to it, so RTData can exceed it. Raising it strengthens the central peak relative to the ripples. | `{"type":"number"}` | `255` |


Cross-option checks: `[{"kind":"bounds","option":"extent"}]`.
